# What this notebook does

`03` measured omeprazole and 5-hydroxyomeprazole in every biological file of
every confirmed dataset. This notebook asks what the corpus as a whole supports,
in two explicitly separated meta-analyses plus the context needed to read them.

- **Context first** (kept from the exploratory pass): what each dataset is, how
  much signal it contributes, and the one hard constraint that shapes
  everything, that an absolute ratio is not comparable across datasets while a
  within-study contrast is.
- **Part A: expanding the classic reverse-metabolomics prevalence analysis.**
  The field reports molecule-by-cohort *detection rates* from MS2 matches. We
  run the same analysis with MS1 propagation and compare MS2 vs MS1 detection
  per compound per cohort. This is presence-based, so it is isomer-immune, and
  it is where the pipeline's value shows most cleanly.
- **Part B: the quantitative strand, and where it stops.** The layer the field
  does not have, built on the proteomics match-between-runs precedent:
  known-negative and known-positive controls on the propagated detections, then
  the within-study contrast as the poolable quantity. Its honest result is
  negative — no ratio contrast survives FDR in any deposit — and the variance
  decomposition says why: the cross-deposit offset is body site far more than
  study, so the ratio is comparable within a matrix and not across them.

**What it deliberately does not do: pool an absolute ratio into a single
cross-cohort estimate.** Most datasets share only a `sex` contrast, so such a
pool would average unlike things. Pooling is a real option but needs a shared,
biologically meaningful contrast the corpus does not yet supply, so it is
described rather than run (final section).

# Load the inputs

```{r load-inputs}
samples  <- read_csv("artifacts/sample_table_all.csv",  show_col_types = FALSE)
datasets <- read_csv("artifacts/datasets-confirmed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Per-file table (not deduped to subjects) + the raw MASST hits: the prevalence
# meta-analysis in Part A is a per-file rate, so it must compare like with like
# (per-file MS1 detection vs per-file MS2/MASST detection).
samples_perfile <- read_csv("artifacts/sample_table_perfile.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
masst_hits      <- read.csv("artifacts/hits_curated.csv", check.names = FALSE,
                            stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# has_metadata flag from 02 (metadata resolved in 01): restrict every analysis
# to files a metadata source covers; record-only files stay out of stratified
# work.
bio_meta_per_ds <- readRDS("artifacts/bio_meta_per_ds.rds")
has_meta_lookup <- unlist(lapply(names(bio_meta_per_ds), function(ds) {
  v <- bio_meta_per_ds[[ds]]
  stats::setNames(as.logical(v), paste0(ds, "|", basename(names(v))))
}))
# Normalise a file name for matching across sources: drop accession prefix,
# extension and case. Valid only where a name carries at most one prefix, which
# the sample tables and hits_curated do. Confirmation output does not: its
# source_file can carry an assay index and a doubled accession, and needs
# norm_file_key(x, bio_files) instead.
fkey <- function(x) tolower(sub("[.][^.]*$", "",
          sub("^(MSV[0-9]+|MTBLS[0-9]+|ST[0-9]+)[_-]", "", basename(as.character(x)))))
```

`sample_table_all.csv` carries one row per subject (`03` de-duplicates files to
subjects where subject metadata exists; where it does not, a row is a file).
Throughout this notebook "sample" means one row of that table, except in Part A
which is explicitly per-file.

```{r short-labels}
# The MetaboLights and Workbench ids carry an assay suffix that makes every axis
# unreadable. Shorten for display only; dataset_id stays the join key.
short_ds <- function(x) sub("_AN[0-9]+$", "", sub("_LC-MS_.*$", "", x))

# Sex is deposited as F/M by three deposits and female/male by the rest, so it
# is harmonised once here rather than per analysis.
harmonise_sex <- function(x) {
  s <- tolower(trimws(as.character(x)))
  dplyr::case_when(startsWith(s, "f") ~ "female",
                   startsWith(s, "m") ~ "male",
                   TRUE ~ NA_character_)
}

# Healthy vs not is an explicit whitelist, never a grepl on "healthy|control":
# that pattern also matches QC injections and inverts the Chagas arms. A label
# in neither list stays NA and drops out of any healthy/not-healthy contrast.
HEALTHY_LV <- c("uninfected", "healthy", "control", "healthy control")
NOTHEAL_LV <- c("t. cruzi infected", "critical covid-19 recovered in icu",
                "non-critical covid-19", "non-covid-19 in icu",
                "non-covid-19 with symptoms", "covid-19")
# Can this deposit's rows be collapsed to people? Two things have to hold, and
# testing only one of them is how this went wrong twice. First, coverage: an id
# on essentially every file can be collapsed on, and the odd unmatched file
# (MSV000091520 has one) becomes its own unit downstream without disturbing
# anything. Second, where coverage is partial, the id has to be corroborated --
# MSV000092754 and 092757 label half their files and no id repeats inside either
# deposit, but all 79 appear in BOTH, which only a person id does. The tempting
# shortcut, "a real subject id repeats", fails on every cross-sectional study in
# the corpus: MSV000091520 gives one id per file and records a distinct sex and
# an age computed to the day behind each of them. It would discard six of the
# nine real designs.
subject_resolved <- function(sid, sibling_ids = NULL) {
  ok <- !is.na(sid) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(sid)))
  if (!any(ok)) return(FALSE)
  if (mean(ok) > 0.9) return(TRUE)
  u <- unique(trimws(as.character(sid[ok])))
  length(u) < sum(ok) ||
    (!is.null(sibling_ids) && length(intersect(u, sibling_ids)) >= 0.5 * length(u))
}

# Ids held by the OTHER deposit of a known same-study pair, keyed by dataset_id.
# Built from related_deposits.csv so the pairing is declared in `01` rather than
# hard-coded here.
sibling_id_map <- local({
  rel <- read.csv("artifacts/related_deposits.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  ids <- function(d) {
    v <- samples_perfile$subject_id[samples_perfile$dataset_id == d]
    unique(trimws(as.character(v[!is.na(v) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(v)))])))
  }
  out <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(rel))) {
    a <- rel$dataset_id[i]; b <- rel$related_to[i]
    out[[a]] <- ids(b); out[[b]] <- ids(a)
  }
  out
})

harmonise_health <- function(x) {
  cl <- tolower(trimws(as.character(x)))
  dplyr::case_when(cl %in% HEALTHY_LV ~ "healthy",
                   cl %in% NOTHEAL_LV ~ "not healthy",
                   TRUE ~ NA_character_)
}
```

# The datasets

## Metadata is the binding constraint

The measurement side of this project is not what limits it. Of 128 deposits
carrying a hit, 12 survive to be measured, and of those only a handful can
answer a question about a person. Every step of that attrition after the
chemistry is a metadata step, and the figure below is the argument for treating
metadata as the bottleneck rather than a preliminary.

```{r fig-metadata-bottleneck, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 3.9}
#| echo: false
.f <- function(v) !is.na(v) & trimws(as.character(v)) != "" & v != "missing value"
.hit <- read.csv("StructureMASST_output/fasstrecords_hits.csv", check.names = FALSE)
.cf  <- read.csv("artifacts/hits-confirmed-all.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
.sp  <- samples_perfile
.sp$repo <- ifelse(startsWith(.sp$dataset_id, "MSV"), "MassIVE",
            ifelse(startsWith(.sp$dataset_id, "MTBLS"), "MetaboLights", "Workbench"))

# Panel A: attrition. The last step is the one that is not about chemistry.
.n_hit  <- dplyr::n_distinct(.hit$ATTRIBUTE_DatasetAccession)
.n_conf <- dplyr::n_distinct(.cf$dataset_id)
.n_subj <- sum(vapply(split(.sp, .sp$dataset_id), function(z)
  subject_resolved(z$subject_id,
    sibling_ids = unlist(sibling_id_map[unique(z$dataset_id)], use.names = FALSE)),
  logical(1)))
.fun <- data.frame(
  step = factor(c("deposits with a hit", "both compounds", "curated entities",
                  "SIRIUS confirmed", "usable subject id"),
                levels = rev(c("deposits with a hit", "both compounds", "curated entities",
                               "SIRIUS confirmed", "usable subject id"))),
  n = c(.n_hit, 44, 15, .n_conf, .n_subj),
  why = c("", "one compound only", "metadata, DIA or in vitro",
          "isobar, or one role only", "no subject recorded"))
.pA <- ggplot(.fun, aes(n, step)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = "grey30") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0, label = why), hjust = -0.03, vjust = 3.1, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "A   Where the corpus is lost",
       subtitle = "only the second step is about chemistry") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8.5, colour = "grey35"))

# Panel B: coverage by repository. Species lives in the search index, not the
# per-file metadata, so it is a share of hits where the others are a share of
# files.
.cov <- .sp |> dplyr::group_by(repo) |> dplyr::summarise(
  `subject id` = mean(.f(subject_id)), sex = mean(.f(sex)),
  age = mean(is.finite(as_num(age))),
  clinical = mean(.f(health_status)), `body site` = mean(.f(body_site)), .groups = "drop")
.hit$repo <- ifelse(startsWith(.hit$ATTRIBUTE_DatasetAccession, "MSV"), "MassIVE",
             ifelse(startsWith(.hit$ATTRIBUTE_DatasetAccession, "MTBLS"), "MetaboLights",
             ifelse(startsWith(.hit$ATTRIBUTE_DatasetAccession, "ST"), "Workbench", NA)))
.spc <- .hit[.hit$ATTRIBUTE_DatasetAccession %in% unique(.cf$deposit_id), ] |>
  dplyr::group_by(repo) |> dplyr::summarise(species = mean(.f(NCBITaxonomy)), .groups = "drop")
.cov <- dplyr::left_join(.cov, .spc, by = "repo") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-repo, names_to = "field", values_to = "cov")
.cov$field <- factor(.cov$field,
  levels = c("subject id", "species", "sex", "age", "clinical", "body site"))
.pB <- ggplot(.cov, aes(field, repo, fill = cov)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cov), colour = cov > 0.5),
            size = 3.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey93", high = "grey25", guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey20")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "B   No repository is adequate on its own, or together",
       subtitle = "share of files carrying the field; species is a share of hits") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8.5, colour = "grey35"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))

.p_meta <- patchwork::wrap_plots(.pA, .pB, ncol = 2)
dir.create("thesis/graphics", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave("thesis/graphics/flagship_metadata_bottleneck.png", .p_meta,
       width = 11, height = 3.9, dpi = 200)
.p_meta
```

Panel B is not an argument for pooling the repositories. Each is strong where
another is empty --- MassIVE records species on a tenth of its hits and sex on
almost all of them, MetaboLights the reverse --- but combining them does not
produce a complete picture, because the gaps are not the same gaps and nothing
fills them. What it shows is that the corpus a researcher can assemble is
bounded by deposition practice, and that no amount of care at the analysis end
recovers a field nobody wrote down.


```{r fig-metadata-inventory, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5.6}
#| echo: false
# Three states per cell, because "recorded" and "usable" differ: a field present
# on every file but holding one value describes the cohort and supports no
# contrast.
.filled <- function(v) !is.na(v) & nzchar(as.character(v))
.inv <- samples_perfile
.inv$ds <- short_ds(.inv$dataset_id)
.inv$clinical <- ifelse(.filled(.inv$health_status), .inv$health_status, .inv$group)
.flds <- c(subject = "subject_id", sex = "sex", age = "age", `body site` = "body_site",
           `clinical group` = "clinical", timepoint = "timepoint",
           treatment = "treatment", country = "country")
.gt <- if (file.exists("artifacts/rescue_samples.csv")) {
  .rs <- read.csv("artifacts/rescue_samples.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if ("cyp2c19_genotype" %in% names(.rs))

.long <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(.flds), function(nm) {
  .inv |> dplyr::group_by(ds) |>
    dplyr::summarise(field = nm, coverage = mean(.filled(.data[[.flds[[nm]]]])),
                     levels = dplyr::n_distinct(.data[[.flds[[nm]]]][.filled(.data[[.flds[[nm]]]])]),
                     .groups = "drop") }))
.long <- dplyr::bind_rows(.long, .inv |> dplyr::group_by(ds) |>
  dplyr::summarise(field = "CYP2C19 genotype",
                   coverage = as.numeric(dplyr::first(ds) %in% .gt),
                   levels = ifelse(dplyr::first(ds) %in% .gt, 5, 0), .groups = "drop"))
# Partial coverage is a legend state, not a footnote symbol: an asterisk needs a
# caption to mean anything, and this figure has to stand on its own.
.long$state <- dplyr::case_when(
  .long$levels == 0 | .long$coverage < 0.4 ~ "not recorded",

  levels > 20 ~ "20+", TRUE ~ as.character(levels)))
.sz <- .inv |> dplyr::group_by(ds) |> dplyr::summarise(files = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")
.long <- dplyr::left_join(.long, .sz, by = "ds")
.long$row <- paste0(.long$ds, "   (", .long$files, " files)")

# Written to thesis/graphics so the chapter figure IS this object. The earlier

.p_inv <- ggplot(.long, aes(field, reorder(row, -rank(ds)), fill = state)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.7) +

                                                   "varies, on all files")),
            size = 3.1, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("not recorded" = "grey95",
                               "recorded, one value only" = "grey80",
                               "varies, but on under 80% of files" = "grey52",
                               "varies, on all files" = "grey20"), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey15")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Metadata fields recorded per deposit, and the number of distinct values in each") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +

```

Before any analysis, the cast. Each row is one confirmed (deposit, assay)
entity: where it came from, what it is, how much usable signal it contributes,
and which grouping variables it offers for a contrast.

A dataset can only support a contrast on a variable with at least two levels
carrying at least three samples each, the same rule `fit_within_study()` applies
below.

One trap is worth naming. A rule written for categorical fields silently
discards continuous ones: a check that lists named categorical candidates
reports `age` as absent everywhere, although it is continuous in five deposits
and the most widely available stratifier in the corpus. Numeric and categorical
fields are therefore judged separately below.

```{r dataset-summary}
#| echo: false
usable_contrasts <- function(df) {
  cand <- c("health_status", "group", "sex", "country", "body_site", "age", "treatment")
  lab <- vapply(cand, function(v) {
    if (!v %in% names(df)) return(NA_character_)
    x <- df[[v]][!is.na(df[[v]])]
    if (!length(x)) return(NA_character_)
    # a predicate, not a coercion: as.numeric() on a categorical field answers the
  # question by raising a warning, which is noise we would then have to hide
  num <- all(grepl("^ *-?[0-9]+[.]?[0-9]*([eE][-+]?[0-9]+)? *$", as.character(x)))
    if (num && dplyr::n_distinct(x) > 12)
      return(sprintf("%s (%.0f-%.0f)", v, min(as.numeric(x)), max(as.numeric(x))))
    tb <- table(x)
    if (length(tb) >= 2 && sum(tb >= 3) >= 2)
      sprintf("%s (%d)", v, length(tb)) else NA_character_
  }, character(1))
  lab <- lab[!is.na(lab)]
  if (!length(lab)) "none" else paste(lab, collapse = ", ")
}

ds_table <- samples |>
  group_by(dataset_id) |>
  summarise(
    n_samples = n(),
    n_both    = sum(detection_tier == "both", na.rm = TRUE),
    both_rate = n_both / n_samples,
    contrasts = usable_contrasts(pick(everything())),
    .groups   = "drop") |>
  left_join(datasets |> select(dataset_id, repository, chromatography,
                               const_country, const_body_site),
            by = "dataset_id") |>
  mutate(dataset = short_ds(dataset_id),
         both_rate = percent(both_rate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  select(dataset, repository, body_site = const_body_site,
         country = const_country, chromatography,
         n_samples, n_both, both_rate, contrasts) |>
  arrange(desc(n_both))

ds_table
```

## What each deposit can and cannot be asked

The table above says what divides a deposit. This one adds what does *not*: a
field present on every file but holding a single value describes the cohort and
supports no contrast, and reporting it as "recorded" would overstate what the
deposit can answer.

```{r metadata-inventory-table}
#| echo: false
FIELDS <- c("sex", "age", "group", "health_status", "body_site", "country",
            "treatment", "subject_id")
describe <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(x)))]
  if (!length(x)) return(list(kind = "absent", lab = NA_character_))
  n <- dplyr::n_distinct(x)
  # a predicate, not a coercion: as.numeric() on a categorical field answers the
  # question by raising a warning, which is noise we would then have to hide
  num <- all(grepl("^ *-?[0-9]+[.]?[0-9]*([eE][-+]?[0-9]+)? *$", as.character(x)))
  if (n == 1) return(list(kind = "constant", lab = as.character(x[1])))
  if (num && n > 12)
    return(list(kind = "divides",
                lab = sprintf("%s (%.0f-%.0f)", "continuous", min(as.numeric(x)),
                              max(as.numeric(x)))))
  list(kind = "divides", lab = sprintf("%d levels", n))
}
inv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(samples, samples$dataset_id), function(d) {
  r <- lapply(FIELDS, function(f) if (f %in% names(d)) describe(d[[f]]) else
                                  list(kind = "absent", lab = NA_character_))
  names(r) <- FIELDS
  data.frame(
    dataset  = short_ds(d$dataset_id[1]),
    divides  = paste(vapply(FIELDS, function(f)
                 if (r[[f]]$kind == "divides") sprintf("%s: %s", f, r[[f]]$lab) else "",
                 character(1))[vapply(r, function(z) z$kind, "") == "divides"],
                 collapse = ", "),
    constant = paste(vapply(FIELDS, function(f)
                 if (r[[f]]$kind == "constant") sprintf("%s=%s", f, r[[f]]$lab) else "",
                 character(1))[vapply(r, function(z) z$kind, "") == "constant"],
                 collapse = ", "),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
inv$divides[inv$divides == ""] <- "nothing"
inv$constant[inv$constant == ""] <- "-"
knitr::kable(inv, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "What divides each deposit, and what merely describes it")
```

Two readings follow from this that matter downstream. Age is the most widely
available stratifier in the corpus, not sex or clinical group, which is the
opposite of what the earlier categorical-only check suggested. And a deposit can
be fully annotated and still answer nothing: MSV000091520 carries sex, age,
group, health status, body site and country on all 2,144 of its files, but every
one of those except age holds a single value, and the compound is detected in 2
files.

Read this table as the corpus' honest capacity. Three things it makes obvious:

- **`n_both` is what the ratio analysis actually runs on.** Everything else is a
  sample where at least one of the two compounds was not detected, so no ratio
  can be formed. Across the whole corpus this number is small, and it is
  concentrated in a few deposits.
- **The deposits are not the same kind of thing.** A couple are drug-probe
  cohorts where every subject was dosed by design. Most are general-population
  or disease cohorts where a handful of people happened to be on omeprazole.
  Those two categories cannot be read the same way.
- **`contrasts` shows what each dataset can be asked.** Note how few offer a
  biologically meaningful grouping. That single column is the reason the last
  section of this notebook exists.

# Exploratory look at the corpus

This section is descriptive on purpose. Before modelling anything, it is worth
seeing what the data look like.

## Detection-tier composition per dataset

Counts on the left, the same thing proportionally on the right. The left panel
shows where the signal actually is; the right panel shows what fraction of each
cohort was exposed.

```{r exp-tier-bars}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| layout-ncol: 2
tier_levels  <- c("both", "parent_only", "metab_only", "neither")
tier_palette <- c(both        = "#1b9e77",
                  parent_only = "#7570b3",
                  metab_only  = "#d95f02",
                  neither     = "grey75")

tier_long <- samples |>
  mutate(detection_tier = factor(detection_tier, levels = tier_levels),
         ds = short_ds(dataset_id)) |>
  count(ds, detection_tier) |>
  group_by(ds) |>
  mutate(p = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(tier_long,
       aes(x = fct_reorder(ds, p * (detection_tier == "both"),
                           .fun = sum, .desc = FALSE),
           y = n, fill = detection_tier)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tier_palette) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "samples", fill = "tier",
       title = "Detection tier, counts") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplot(tier_long,
       aes(x = fct_reorder(ds, p * (detection_tier == "both"),
                           .fun = sum, .desc = FALSE),
           y = p, fill = detection_tier)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tier_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "share of samples", fill = "tier",
       title = "Detection tier, proportional") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The `parent_only` and `metab_only` slices are censored ratio observations, not
failures: we know the ratio is very high or very low, but not by how much,
because one peak fell below detection. Discarding them biases any ratio estimate
toward the middle, which is a point the final section returns to.

## Deposit size vs detection rate

```{r exp-n-vs-both, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5}
ds_summary <- samples |>
  group_by(dataset_id) |>
  summarise(n_samples = n(),
            n_both    = sum(detection_tier == "both"),
            both_rate = n_both / n_samples,
            .groups   = "drop") |>
  left_join(datasets |> select(dataset_id, chromatography,
                               const_country, const_body_site),
            by = "dataset_id")

ggplot(ds_summary, aes(x = n_samples, y = both_rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_both, colour = chromatography), alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = short_ds(dataset_id)), size = 3,
                  min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 8)) +
  labs(x = "samples in deposit (log10)", y = "'both' detection rate",
       size = "n with both",
       title = "Deposit size vs detection rate") +
  theme_bw()
```

The two axes trade off against each other. The drug-probe cohorts sit top-left
(small but almost fully exposed); the large unselected cohorts sit bottom-right
(many subjects, almost none on the drug). A large deposit with a low rate can
still be worth having, but only if the absolute number of exposed subjects is
large enough to matter, which is the `n_both` point size rather than the
position.

## Parent vs metabolite intensity

```{r exp-auc-scatter, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5.5}
auc_df <- samples |>
  filter(detection_tier == "both", par_auc > 0, met_auc > 0) |>
  mutate(ds = short_ds(dataset_id))

ggplot(auc_df, aes(x = par_auc, y = met_auc, colour = ds)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.4) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "parent peak area (log10)", y = "metabolite peak area (log10)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Per-sample parent vs metabolite intensity") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The dashed line is `y = x`. Points below it have more parent than metabolite.
Note the datasets separate into visible clusters. What the clusters are made of
is the question the next section takes up: deposits differ in instrument,
gradient and specimen at once, and nothing here tells them apart.

## Peak-quality control

```{r exp-fwhm-qc, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5}
peak_qc <- samples |>
  filter(detection_tier == "both") |>
  mutate(ds = short_ds(dataset_id)) |>
  select(ds, par_fwhm, met_fwhm) |>
  pivot_longer(c(par_fwhm, met_fwhm), names_to = "role", values_to = "fwhm") |>
  mutate(role = sub("_fwhm", "", role))

ggplot(peak_qc |> filter(is.finite(fwhm)), aes(x = fwhm, y = ds, colour = role)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") +
  labs(x = "peak width at half maximum (s, log10)", y = NULL, colour = "role",
       title = "Peak-width distribution per dataset") +
  theme_bw()
```

Peak width is a chromatography property. A dataset whose widths sit far from the
rest, or whose two compounds disagree with each other, is worth a second look in
its per-dataset report before its numbers are trusted.

# What we can and cannot compare across datasets

This is the central constraint of the whole project, so it is worth stating
precisely.

A mass spectrometer counts ions, not molecules. How many ions a compound yields
depends on how readily it ionises, which is a property of the molecule **and**
of the method. Omeprazole and 5-hydroxyomeprazole ionise with different
efficiency, so what we measure is

```
measured log2(parent / metabolite) = true log2(parent / metabolite) + offset
```

where `offset` is the log ratio of the two compounds' response factors. It is
unknown, and it is different in every dataset, because every dataset used a
different instrument and method. The standard fix is to spike an
isotope-labelled internal standard of each compound into every sample. **No
deposit in this corpus did that**, so the offset cannot be calibrated away.

That term is established analytical chemistry rather than an assumption of ours.
Oss et al. measured an electrospray ionisation-efficiency scale for 62 organic
compounds and found it spans roughly six orders of magnitude under identical
conditions ([Anal. Chem. 2010, 82(7),
2865-2872](https://doi.org/10.1021/ac902856t)), and follow-up work from the same
group shows the scale is itself condition- and instrument-dependent ([Rapid
Commun. Mass Spectrom. 2021, 35, e9178](https://doi.org/10.1002/rcm.9178)) --
which is why the offset cannot be assumed constant across deposits. Six orders
of magnitude does not sink the ratio, for two reasons: that spread is across 62
*unrelated* compounds, whereas for one fixed pair the offset is a single unknown
constant, and the ratio is itself the normalisation, cancelling everything the
two compounds share in a sample -- injected amount, dilution, most matrix
suppression -- and leaving only that constant.

Two consequences follow, and they are the reason this notebook is shaped the way
it is.

**We cannot compare absolute ratios between datasets.** A dataset whose median
sits a unit above another's may simply have used a method that ionises the
parent more efficiently. Any ranking of the deposits by their ratio would be
measuring instruments, not patients. This is why none of the plots above are
sorted by median.

The corpus does contain two designs that let this be probed rather than merely
asserted: one deposit pair ran the **same subjects on two chromatographies**,
and the probe study sampled **two matrices from the same subjects**. Part A
returns to them under "The ratio across cohorts". The short version is that the
first is too small to pin the offset down, so the constraint above stands
unchanged, while the second removes the offset by construction and is where the
cross-matrix result comes from.

**We can compare a difference measured inside a single dataset.** Within one
dataset every sample went through the same method, so every sample carries the
same `offset`. Take two groups in that dataset and subtract:

```
(true_case + offset) - (true_ref + offset) = true_case - true_ref
```

The offset cancels exactly. That difference, which we will call the
**within-study contrast**, is free of the method term and is therefore the only
quantity in this corpus that means the same thing in every dataset. It underpins
the quantitative analyses in Part B.

<!-- moved ahead of Part A: this is the control that licenses every
prevalence claim below, so it has to be read first. -->
# Does a propagated detection mean anything? The false-transfer rate

Our pipeline is the metabolomics analogue of **match-between-runs (MBR)** in
proteomics: identify by MS2 where a feature was fragmented, then transfer the
identity to other files by accurate mass and retention time and quantify at MS1.
Proteomics has measured what this costs. In a controlled two-species experiment,
uncontrolled MBR transferred 44% of one organism's proteins into samples that
provably did not contain it, concentrated in low-abundance one-hit detections
(Lim, Paulo & Gygi 2019). Independent audits find that the common tools do not
actually control the false-discovery rate of propagated identities unless a
decoy procedure is added (PIP-ECHO, 2025).

The lesson transfers exactly: **a propagated detection is a hypothesis until its
false-transfer rate is estimated.** Part A's prevalence gains are only as
trustworthy as our specificity, and specificity has to be measured, not assumed.

Proteomics measures it with a decoy that **cannot be true** — a reversed or
shuffled peptide sequence, or an entrapment proteome from a species that is not
in the sample — and it scores a match on fragment evidence, charge and isotope
envelope together. An MS1 extraction has neither property. It asks only whether
an acceptable chromatographic peak sits at one m/z inside one retention-time
window, and in an untargeted file real compounds occupy arbitrary masses. So a
synthetic decoy mass is *not* a hypothesis that cannot be true: when it fires,
the picker has usually found a real but different compound, which is the picker
working correctly rather than a false transfer. We measured this directly —
probing the metabolite's own window at +8 and +12 Da returns peaks that are not
isotopologues of anything we search for, i.e. ordinary matrix. **A synthetic
decoy therefore bounds our false-positive rate from above without estimating
it**, so it is not reported here.

Two controls are used instead, and both rest on files whose true answer is known
rather than assumed:

- **positive control** — every file carrying a SIRIUS-confirmed spectrum, which
  is known to contain the compound. Anything the extraction fails to recover is
  a false negative. This measures sensitivity.
- **negative biological control** — the pre-dose plasma draws of the probe
  study, taken before the drug was given, interrogated at the true m/z and the
  true retention window. Real matrix, every interference a study sample carries,
  absence known by design. This is the closest thing the corpus offers to an
  entrapment experiment, and it measures specificity where it actually matters.

```{r fig-decoy, fig.width = 6.4, fig.height = 3.6}
#| echo: false
# Positive-control counts are recomputed here from the SIRIUS-confirmed anchor
# files rather than transcribed.
{
  # Runs before Part A builds pf, so it works from the per-file table directly,
  # and is not restricted to metadata-carrying files: the positive control
  # concerns the extraction. norm_file_key with the deposit's file list, never
  # the bare fkey() -- confirmation names can carry a doubled accession, and the
  # bare rule lost 39 confirmed files here.
  .BFp <- readRDS("artifacts/bio_files_per_ds.rds")
  .bare <- function(x, ds) {
    r <- character(length(x))
    for (d in unique(ds)) {
      i <- ds == d
      ref <- if (!is.null(.BFp[[d]])) basename(as.character(.BFp[[d]])) else NULL
      r[i] <- norm_file_key(x[i], ref)
    }
    r
  }
  .sp  <- as.data.frame(samples_perfile)
  .pfk <- .bare(.sp$file, .sp$dataset_id)
  .conf <- read.csv("artifacts/hits-confirmed-all.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  .conf$fk <- .bare(.conf$source_file, .conf$dataset_id)
  .pc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(par = "parent", met = "metabolite"), function(r) {
    keys <- unique(paste0(.conf$dataset_id[.conf$role == r], "|", .conf$fk[.conf$role == r]))
    x <- .sp[paste0(.sp$dataset_id, "|", .pfk) %in% keys, ]
    hit <- if (r == "parent") x$detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only") else
                              x$detection_tier %in% c("both", "metab_only")
    data.frame(n = nrow(x), det = sum(hit))
  }))

  # Two controls, both on samples whose true answer is known. Split by role,
  # because the metabolite is harder to recover and a pooled bar could hide a
  # shortfall in it. Labelled positive/negative control rather than
  # sensitivity/specificity: the y axis is a detection rate, so the negative bar
  # reads 0% where specificity would read 100%.
  POS <- "positive control: present"
  NEG <- "negative control: absent"
  .rows <- rbind(
    data.frame(cond = "confirmed\nparent",     n = .pc["par", "n"], det = .pc["par", "det"],
               grp = POS),
    data.frame(cond = "confirmed\nmetabolite", n = .pc["met", "n"], det = .pc["met", "det"],
               grp = POS),
    # Pre-dose plasma, counted from the extracted files rather than written in:
    # the submitter TSV declares 50 draws and 49 were extracted.
    local({
      # Both draws precede absorption, so both are known negatives. Pooling them
      # is what tightens the bound: zero of n only says as much as n allows.
      .pre <- .sp[.sp$dataset_id == "MSV000084008" & .sp$timepoint %in% c("0", "5"), ]
      data.frame(cond = "pre-dose and\n5 min plasma", n = nrow(.pre),
                 det = sum(.pre$detection_tier != "neither"), grp = NEG)
    }))
  .rows$rate <- .rows$det / .rows$n
  # Exact binomial interval. It is what turns "no false positives" into a
  # bounded false-positive rate, and 768 of 771 into a recovery with a floor.
  .rows$lo <- NA_real_; .rows$hi <- NA_real_
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(.rows))) {
    ct <- binom.test(.rows$det[i], .rows$n[i])
    .rows$lo[i] <- ct$conf.int[1]; .rows$hi[i] <- ct$conf.int[2]
  }
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(.rows)))
    cat(sprintf("%-26s %4d/%-4d = %5.1f%%  (95%% CI %.1f%% to %.1f%%)\n",
                gsub("[\r\n]+", " ", .rows$cond[i]), .rows$det[i], .rows$n[i],
                100 * .rows$rate[i], 100 * .rows$lo[i], 100 * .rows$hi[i]))
  .rows$cond <- factor(.rows$cond, levels = .rows$cond)
  .rows$grp  <- factor(.rows$grp,  levels = c(POS, NEG))

  ggplot(.rows, aes(cond, rate)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.55, fill = "grey25") +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d / %d", det, n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.3) +
    facet_grid(~ grp, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.12),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "files with a detection") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey93", colour = NA),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5)) -> .p_ctl
  dir.create("thesis/graphics", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  ggsave("thesis/graphics/flagship_decoy.png", .p_ctl, width = 6.4, height = 3.6, dpi = 200)
  .p_ctl
}
```

The two controls fail in opposite directions and both come back clean. The
confirmed files re-detect at MS1 at the rates the figure gives, so the gating
loses almost nothing that MS2 had already established. In the pre-dose plasma
draws — real matrix, true m/z, true retention window, drug absent by design —
the extraction finds nothing. Both counts are computed in the chunk above rather
than written into this paragraph: the earlier hand-written pair (82 and 106) was
left behind by the uncapped re-confirmation and understated the control by
nearly an order of magnitude.

That is what licenses Part A: the prevalence gains that follow are a gain in
sensitivity rather than an accumulation of false positives.

It licenses less than a decoy-based figure would, and the difference should be
stated rather than glossed. The negative control is 49 files from one cohort, so
it constrains the false-positive rate in dosed-study plasma, not across the
corpus, and no comparable known-negative exists for the other eleven deposits or
for urine, faeces and skin. Proteomics can quote a corpus-wide false-transfer
rate (IonQuant measures 2.3% at a nominal 1% FDR, Yu 2021) because a reversed
peptide sequence is knowably false in *every* run; nothing in an untargeted
metabolomics archive is knowably absent in every file. Closing that gap needs
cohorts with a documented unexposed arm, not a better statistic.


# Part A: What propagation adds, per dataset and across the corpus

## What the field does, and how we extend it

The reverse-metabolomics / MASST tools answer one question at repository scale:
in what fraction of files does a molecule appear? Their cross-cohort output is a
**prevalence table or heatmap** of molecule-by-cohort detection rates, built
from MS2 spectral matches, and used strictly for hypothesis generation. They
never quantify intensity across deposits, and their own authors state that a
negative result is not evidence of absence, because a compound present at low
abundance may never be selected for fragmentation.

That last point is exactly the gap MS1 propagation fills. We run the same
prevalence analysis, but replace "did a file get an MS2 match?" with "does the
compound's signal appear at its confirmed mass and retention time?", which is
recorded for every file whether or not the instrument fragmented it. So Part A
is the field's own analysis at higher sensitivity: **per compound, per cohort,
the MS2 detection rate versus the MS1-propagated detection rate.** It rests on
presence, not on a quantity, so it is immune to the response-factor and isobaric
problems that constrain the ratio.

One unit note: prevalence is a **per-file** rate, so this section uses the
per-file table (not the subject-deduped one) and compares it to the per-file
MASST hits, restricted to files a metadata source covers.

```{r prevalence-setup}
#| echo: false
pf <- samples_perfile
pf$has_metadata <- {
  k <- paste0(pf$dataset_id, "|", basename(as.character(pf$file)))
  h <- has_meta_lookup[k]; ifelse(is.na(h), FALSE, unname(h))
}
pf <- pf[pf$has_metadata %in% TRUE, ]
pf$fk <- fkey(pf$file)

# MS2 baseline: metadata-carrying files with a MASST hit of each role. Restrict
# the hits to the same file universe (dataset_id | normalised key) so MS2 and
# MS1 rates share a denominator.
valid_dk       <- paste0(pf$dataset_id, "|", pf$fk)
masst_hits$fk  <- fkey(masst_hits$file_path)
masst_hits$dk  <- paste0(masst_hits$dataset_id, "|", masst_hits$fk)
mh_valid       <- masst_hits[masst_hits$dk %in% valid_dk, ]

# The ONE deposit pair that is the same study under two accessions, identified
# from subject identity: the same 14 subjects, and on every shared file the
# subject, timepoint, study day and body site agree 461/461. One physical file
# shared by that pair must count ONCE. Rows from the pair share a namespace;
# every other deposit keeps its own, so identical names across unrelated
# deposits never merge.
DUP_STUDY <- c("MSV000082493", "MSV000084008")
dup_key <- function(dataset_id, fk)
  ifelse(dataset_id %in% DUP_STUDY, paste0("DUPSTUDY|", fk),
         paste0(dataset_id, "|", fk))


ms2 <- mh_valid |>
  dplyr::distinct(dataset_id, role, fk) |>
  dplyr::count(dataset_id, role, name = "ms2") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = role, values_from = ms2, values_fill = 0)
if (!"parent"     %in% names(ms2)) ms2$parent     <- 0L
if (!"metabolite" %in% names(ms2)) ms2$metabolite <- 0L

# A file supports a RATIO only when both compounds are present, so that is
# counted separately: it is the quantity the downstream ratio work actually
# depends on.
ms2_both <- mh_valid |>
  dplyr::distinct(dataset_id, role, fk) |>
  dplyr::count(dataset_id, fk, name = "n_roles") |>
  dplyr::filter(n_roles == 2) |>
  dplyr::count(dataset_id, name = "both")

prevalence <- pf |>
  dplyr::group_by(dataset_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_files        = dplyr::n(),
                   ms1_parent     = sum(detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only")),
                   ms1_metabolite = sum(detection_tier %in% c("both", "metab_only")),
                   ms1_both       = sum(detection_tier == "both"),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::left_join(ms2_both, by = "dataset_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(both = tidyr::replace_na(as.integer(both), 0L)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ms2, by = "dataset_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(parent, metabolite),
                              ~ tidyr::replace_na(as.integer(.), 0L)),
                ds = short_ds(dataset_id))

prev_long <- prevalence |>
  dplyr::transmute(ds, n_files,
    `omeprazole (MS2)`          = parent        / n_files,
    `omeprazole (MS1)`          = ms1_parent    / n_files,
    `5-OH-omeprazole (MS2)`     = metabolite    / n_files,
    `5-OH-omeprazole (MS1)`     = ms1_metabolite / n_files) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(ds, n_files), names_to = "panel", values_to = "rate") |>
  tidyr::separate(panel, into = c("compound", "method"), sep = " \\(") |>
  dplyr::mutate(method = sub("\\)", "", method))
```

## The prevalence heatmap: MS2 versus MS1, per compound, per cohort

This is the figure that shows what the pipeline buys. Each row is a cohort, each
column a (compound, detection-method) pair; colour is the fraction of that
cohort's files in which the compound is detected. The MS1 columns should be at
least as dark as their MS2 counterparts, and much darker wherever the instrument
under-fragmented the compound.

```{r prevalence-heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
prev_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(col = paste0(compound, "\n", method),
                col = factor(col, levels = c(
                  "omeprazole\nMS2", "omeprazole\nMS1",
                  "5-OH-omeprazole\nMS2", "5-OH-omeprazole\nMS1"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = col, y = reorder(ds, rate, sum), fill = rate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 1)), size = 2.7) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "#1b6837",
                      labels = scales::percent, name = "detection\nrate") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Files with a detection per cohort, MASST MS2 and MS1-propagated") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(lineheight = 0.9))
```

## The propagation gain per cohort

The same numbers as a gain: MS1 detections divided by MS2 detections, per
compound per cohort. This is the honest, cohort-resolved version of the
propagation-gain headline (a single corpus-wide multiplier hides that the gain
is largest exactly where MS2 coverage is thinnest).

A cohort whose MS2 baseline is zero inside the analysed files has **no defined
gain**: a ratio needs a denominator. Printing `x / max(0, 1)` would invent one,
so those cells read `n/a` and the counts alone carry the meaning.

**MSV000082433 (\*) needs its own note, because it is not a gain at all.** Its
entire MS2 evidence for both roles is a single file, `957.mzML`, which sits on
`20161103_Amerindian_Plate6`. Pan-ReDU indexes only plates 1 to 3 of this
deposit, so that file is described by no metadata source, and the MS2 columns
above, which are restricted to annotated files, cannot count it. The file itself
is not the problem: it carries a clean, textbook omeprazole peak (1.1e8 at the
confirmed retention time) and a confirmed 5-OH peak. It is simply unusable,
because without metadata it cannot enter any stratified analysis.

```{r ds82433-parent}
#| echo: false
# Counted, not written in: this pair read "219 of 224" for a while after a
# re-extraction moved it.
.x433 <- samples_perfile[samples_perfile$dataset_id == "MSV000082433", ]
N433_NOPEAK <- sum(is.na(.x433$par_auc)); N433_FILES <- nrow(.x433)
```

Inside the annotated files the picture is the opposite. The parent produces **no
chromatographic peak** at the confirmed retention time in `r N433_NOPEAK` of
`r N433_FILES` files; the handful of files with any in-window signal show
single-scan spikes (one point at 0.5 to 0.83 s scan spacing, with nothing on
either side), which the point-count gate correctly rejects. So the metabolite
counts for this cohort are a presence observation with **no parent, no ratio,
and no MS2 baseline to compare against**. Read that row as "one confirmed but
unannotated file, plus a metabolite-only presence signal", never as a
propagation gain.

```{r prevalence-gain}
#| echo: false
gain_str <- function(ms2, ms1) {
  ifelse(ms2 > 0,
         sprintf("%d -> %d  (%.1fx)", ms2, ms1, ms1 / pmax(ms2, 1)),
         sprintf("%d -> %d  (n/a: no MS2 in analysed files)", ms2, ms1))
}
prevalence |>
  dplyr::transmute(cohort = ifelse(ds == "MSV000082433", paste0(ds, " *"), ds), n_files,
    `omeprazole: MS2 -> MS1` = gain_str(parent, ms1_parent),
    `5-OH: MS2 -> MS1`       = gain_str(metabolite, ms1_metabolite),
    # a ratio needs both compounds in one file, so it is counted here rather
    # than inferred from the two columns beside it
    `usable ratio: MS2 -> MS1` = gain_str(both, ms1_both)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n_files))

write_csv(dplyr::arrange(prevalence, dplyr::desc(n_files)),
          "artifacts/prevalence_by_deposit.csv")
```

Detecting one compound is not the same as being able to compute a ratio, which
needs both in the same file. That is the number the whole quantitative strand
rests on, so it is counted separately rather than inferred from the two columns
above.

**No file is counted twice.** MSV000082493 and MSV000084008 share 333 physical
files; those contribute once, so the totals below are over distinct files.
Simply summing the per-cohort rows above would have counted them twice and
inflated every number.

```{r propagation-corpus-totals}
#| echo: false
pfd <- pf
pfd$dk <- dup_key(pfd$dataset_id, pfd$fk)
pfd <- pfd[!duplicated(pfd$dk), ]                    # one row per physical file

mhd <- mh_valid
mhd$dk <- dup_key(mhd$dataset_id, mhd$fk)
ms2_n <- function(r) length(unique(mhd$dk[mhd$role == r]))
ms2_both_n <- length(intersect(mhd$dk[mhd$role == "parent"],
                               mhd$dk[mhd$role == "metabolite"]))

tot <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("omeprazole", "5-OH-omeprazole", "both, i.e. a usable ratio"),
  MASST_MS2 = c(ms2_n("parent"), ms2_n("metabolite"), ms2_both_n),
  MS1_propagated = c(sum(pfd$detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only")),
                     sum(pfd$detection_tier %in% c("both", "metab_only")),
                     sum(pfd$detection_tier == "both")))
tot$gain <- sprintf("%.2fx", tot$MS1_propagated / tot$MASST_MS2)

# An interval on the gain, resampling DEPOSITS rather than files. Files inside a
# deposit share its chromatography, its depositor and its detection rate, so they
# are not independent draws and a file-level bootstrap reports an interval far
# tighter than the evidence supports. Twelve deposits is the real sample size.
set.seed(1)
.dep <- unique(pfd$dataset_id)
.gboot <- replicate(2000, {
  d <- sample(.dep, replace = TRUE)
  # A deposit drawn twice must count twice, so each draw carries its own tag;
  # without it unique()/intersect() would silently collapse the duplicate and the
  # resample would be a subsample.
  tag <- function(tb, j) {
    x <- tb[tb$dataset_id == d[j], , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(x)) x$dk <- paste0(j, "|", x$dk)
    x
  }
  p2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(d), function(j) tag(pfd, j)))
  m2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(d), function(j) tag(mhd, j)))
  ms1 <- c(sum(p2$detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only")),
           sum(p2$detection_tier %in% c("both", "metab_only")),
           sum(p2$detection_tier == "both"))
  # distinct FILES, matching how the point estimate is counted
  ms2 <- c(length(unique(m2$dk[m2$role == "parent"])),
           length(unique(m2$dk[m2$role == "metabolite"])),
           length(intersect(unique(m2$dk[m2$role == "parent"]),
                            unique(m2$dk[m2$role == "metabolite"]))))
  ifelse(ms2 > 0, ms1 / ms2, NA_real_)
})
.q <- apply(.gboot, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
tot$gain_ci <- sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", .q[1, ], .q[2, ])
knitr::kable(tot, caption = sprintf(paste(
  "Files with a detection, %d distinct metadata-carrying files across 12 deposits.",
  "The gain interval is a bootstrap over deposits, not files."),
  nrow(pfd)))
```

The ratio row is the one that matters: a file needs **both** compounds before it
can say anything quantitative, and that is where propagation helps most, because
it can rescue either compound in a file where MS2 caught only the other one.

## The resource this produces, deposit by deposit

The totals say how much was recovered. They do not say where it landed, and for
anyone deciding whether these data are worth reusing that is the more useful
question. So the same output is described three ways below: how many independent
units carry a ratio, what the ratio's level is in each deposit, and which strata
each deposit could be cut by.

The unit here is one row per subject per deposit, taking the median over that
subject's files. Three deposits record no subject, so there the file is the unit
and the count is an upper bound on the number of people rather than a number of
people.

```{r output-units}
#| echo: false
DUP_LABEL <- "MSV000082493/084008"

rr <- pf[pf$detection_tier == "both" & is.finite(pf$log2_ratio), ]
rr$dk    <- dup_key(rr$dataset_id, rr$fk)
rr       <- rr[!duplicated(rr$dk), ]
rr$study <- ifelse(rr$dataset_id %in% DUP_STUDY, DUP_LABEL, rr$dataset_id)
rr$has_subject <- !is.na(rr$subject_id) & rr$subject_id != ""
rr$unit  <- ifelse(rr$has_subject, paste0("S:", rr$study, "|", rr$subject_id),
                   paste0("F:", rr$study, "|", rr$dk))

ratio_units <- rr |>
  dplyr::group_by(study, unit) |>
  dplyr::summarise(log2_ratio  = median(log2_ratio),
                   has_subject = all(has_subject),
                   n_files     = dplyr::n(),
                   sex         = dplyr::first(sex),
                   health      = dplyr::first(health_status),
                   age         = as_num(dplyr::first(age)),
                   .groups     = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(ds = short_ds(study))

out_tbl <- ratio_units |>
  dplyr::group_by(ds) |>
  dplyr::summarise(units       = dplyr::n(),
                   files       = sum(n_files),
                   unit_is     = ifelse(all(has_subject), "subject", "file"),
                   median_log2 = round(median(log2_ratio), 2),
                   IQR         = round(IQR(log2_ratio), 2),
                   sex         = sum(!is.na(harmonise_sex(sex))),
                   health      = sum(!is.na(harmonise_health(health))),
                   age         = sum(is.finite(age)),
                   .groups     = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(units))
knitr::kable(out_tbl, caption = sprintf(
  "Units carrying a usable ratio: %d across %d studies. The last three columns count units whose deposit records that field in a form a contrast can use.",
  nrow(ratio_units), dplyr::n_distinct(ratio_units$ds)))
write.csv(out_tbl, "artifacts/output_resource_by_deposit.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

`r nrow(out_tbl)` studies carry at least one ratio, `r sum(out_tbl$units)` units
in total, and only MSV000082433 carries none. That is the resource: small, but
it did not exist before the extraction, since a ratio needs both compounds in
one file and MS2 supplied that in `r ms2_both_n` files, concentrated almost
entirely in the dosed cohort.

Two of those rows are not independent of each other. MSV000092754 and
MSV000092757 are the same subject panel measured twice, by HILIC and by reverse
phase, so they contribute
`r sum(out_tbl$units[out_tbl$ds %in% c("MSV000092754", "MSV000092757")])` units
but not that many people; they are kept apart because the two measurements
differ, not because the two deposits do.

The second column is the reason the corpus cannot simply be pooled. The median
level differs by deposit far more than it differs between people inside a
deposit. Deposits differ in instrument, gradient and specimen at once, so one
median carries all three and this figure separates none of them. The variance
decomposition further down does, and the answer is not the one the
response-factor argument predicts.

```{r fig-ratio-by-dataset, fig.width = 7.6, fig.height = 4.4}

  dplyr::summarise(m = median(log2_ratio), .groups = "drop") |>

ratio_units$ds <- factor(ratio_units$ds, levels = ord$ds)

p_ratio_ds <- ggplot(ratio_units, aes(x = log2_ratio, y = ds)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.55, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey35") +
  geom_jitter(aes(shape = has_subject), height = 0.16, width = 0, alpha = 0.7, size = 1.7) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = "subject", `FALSE` = "file (no subject recorded)"),
                     name = "unit") +
  labs(x = expression(log[2]*"(omeprazole / 5-OH-omeprazole)"), y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p_ratio_ds
ggsave("thesis/graphics/flagship_ratio_by_dataset.png", p_ratio_ds,
       width = 7.6, height = 4.4, dpi = 200)
```

A boxplot per deposit rather than a pooled one, because pooling these would
average over whatever the between-deposit difference is made of and produce a
number that describes no cohort. Within a deposit the spread is what a contrast
can work with; between deposits it is not yet interpretable. That distinction is
what separates the next two sections.

```{r fig-output-strata, fig.width = 8.2, fig.height = 3.6}

str_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  ratio_units |> dplyr::transmute(ds, field = "sex", value = harmonise_sex(sex)),
  ratio_units |> dplyr::transmute(ds, field = "health status", value = harmonise_health(health)),
  ratio_units |> dplyr::transmute(ds, field = "age",
                            value = cut(age, c(-Inf, 40, 60, Inf),
                                        labels = c("<40", "40-59", ">=60"),
                                        right = FALSE) |> as.character())) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(field = factor(field, levels = c("sex", "health status", "age")),
                value = factor(value, levels = LV))

p_strata <- ggplot(str_long, aes(y = ds, fill = value)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ field, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "units carrying a ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"))
p_strata
ggsave("thesis/graphics/flagship_output_strata.png", p_strata,
       width = 8.2, height = 3.6, dpi = 200)

knitr::kable(str_long |> dplyr::count(field, value, name = "units"),
             caption = "Stratifier levels available across the ratio-bearing units")
```

Timepoint is deliberately absent. It is recorded almost only in the dosed
cohort, where it is the design rather than a stratifier, and including it would
have made the corpus look richer in covariates than it is.

Sex is harmonised before counting: three deposits write `F`/`M` and the rest
`female`/`male`, which would otherwise be four levels rather than two. Health
status is mapped through the same explicit whitelist the covariate scan uses, so
labels that are neither clearly healthy nor clearly a disease arm — `chronic
illness`, `compensated`, `decompensated` — stay unset instead of being forced
onto one side.

The fields that survive are thin and unevenly spread, and no field is recorded
across all ten studies. This is the ceiling on everything the next two sections
attempt, and it is a property of what depositors wrote down rather than of the
extraction.

## The analysis unit, and the designs the corpus actually has

Everything from here on is epidemiology rather than extraction, so the unit
changes. The prevalence and gain tables above count **files**, correctly,
because propagation is a per-injection operation. A statistical contrast is a
different question and needs a unit that corresponds to an independent
observation.

Three things sit between a file and an independent observation, and each has
bitten this analysis at some point:

1. **Replicate injections.** One physical sample can be run several times.
2. **Repeated measures within subject.** The probe cohort is 1,137 files from
   **14 people**, about 27 rows each, and every one of those people appears in
   several body sites. Testing body site against detection on the raw rows
   treats one person as 27 observations and returns a p-value that means
   nothing.
3. **Deposits that record no subject at all.** Three do. There a file is the
   only available unit and the design is simply unknown, which has to be said
   rather than assumed away.

The rule used below: **one row per subject per level of the contrast**. A
subject sampled at ten timepoints contributes one observation; a subject sampled
in four matrices contributes one observation *per matrix*, which is correct
because body site is the thing being contrasted. Where no subject is recorded
the file is the unit and the result is flagged `design unknown` and never
reported as confirmatory.

```{r unit-setup}
# One file universe, MS1 and MS2 flags, independent studies rather than
# accessions.
ms2_keys <- unique(paste0(mh_valid$dataset_id, "|", mh_valid$fk))
pm <- pf
pm$ms2 <- paste0(pm$dataset_id, "|", pm$fk) %in% ms2_keys
pm$ms1 <- pm$detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only", "metab_only")
pm$par_ms1 <- pm$detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only")
pm$met_ms1 <- pm$detection_tier %in% c("both", "metab_only")
par_keys <- unique(paste0(mh_valid$dataset_id, "|", mh_valid$fk)[mh_valid$role == "parent"])
met_keys <- unique(paste0(mh_valid$dataset_id, "|", mh_valid$fk)[mh_valid$role == "metabolite"])
pm$par_ms2 <- paste0(pm$dataset_id, "|", pm$fk) %in% par_keys
pm$met_ms2 <- paste0(pm$dataset_id, "|", pm$fk) %in% met_keys

# DUP_STUDY / dup_key are defined with the MS2 baseline above, where the
# reasoning is set out once. The appendix documents the evidence.

pm$study <- dplyr::case_when(
  grepl(paste(DUP_STUDY, collapse = "|"), pm$dataset_id) ~ "Jarmusch probe",
  grepl("MSV000092754|MSV000092757", pm$dataset_id)      ~ "Chagas serum",
  TRUE ~ short_ds(pm$dataset_id))
pm <- pm[!duplicated(paste(pm$study, pm$fk)), ]

nz <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v) | !nzchar(as.character(v)), NA_character_, as.character(v))
pm$subj <- nz(pm$subject_id)

# Deposits name the same matrix differently: blood_plasma and "blood plasma",
# UANoAdditive_YellowTop and urine, fecal and feces. Left raw, one matrix splits
# into several rows of any cross-cohort table and each row reads as a different
# biology.
canon_site <- function(x) {
  y <- tolower(trimws(gsub("[_.]+", " ", as.character(x))))
  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(y) | !nzchar(y)               ~ NA_character_,
    grepl("plasma", y)                  ~ "plasma",
    grepl("serum", y)                   ~ "serum",
    grepl("^ua|urine", y)               ~ "urine",
    grepl("fecal|feces|faec|stool", y)  ~ "faeces",
    grepl("forehead|arm skin|^skin", y) ~ "skin",
    grepl("saliva", y)                  ~ "saliva",
    grepl("oral cavity|mouth", y)       ~ "oral cavity",
    grepl("milk", y)                    ~ "milk",
    grepl("nasal", y)                   ~ "nasal cavity",
    grepl("vagina", y)                  ~ "vagina",
    grepl("anal", y)                    ~ "anal region",
    TRUE                                ~ y)
}
pm$site  <- canon_site(pm$body_site)
pm$sex2  <- dplyr::case_when(grepl("^f", tolower(trimws(pm$sex))) ~ "female",
                             grepl("^m", tolower(trimws(pm$sex))) ~ "male",
                             TRUE ~ NA_character_)
pm$clin  <- ifelse(!is.na(nz(pm$health_status)), pm$health_status, pm$group)
pm$agen  <- as_num(pm$age)
pm$ageb  <- as.character(cut(pm$agen, c(-Inf, 40, 60, Inf),
                             labels = c("<40", "40-60", ">60")))

# The unit rule. Returns one row per (subject, level of g), with the detection
# columns OR-ed within that unit, and records whether the design is
# subject-resolved.
units_for <- function(x, g, cols) {
  keep <- !is.na(g) & nzchar(g)
  x <- x[keep, , drop = FALSE]; g <- g[keep]
  if (!nrow(x)) return(NULL)
  # Per row, not per deposit: a file with no subject is its own unit, since
  # collapsing the unlabelled rows of a partly-labelled deposit would invent one
  # subject per level.
  known <- subject_resolved(x$subj, sibling_ids = unlist(sibling_id_map[unique(x$dataset_id)], use.names = FALSE))
  u <- ifelse(is.na(x$subj), paste0("file:", x$fk), paste(x$subj, g))
  out <- data.frame(unit = u, g = g, x[, cols, drop = FALSE]) |>
    dplyr::group_by(unit) |>
    dplyr::summarise(g = dplyr::first(g),
                     dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(cols), any), .groups = "drop")
  attr(out, "design") <- if (!known) "design unknown"
    else if (any(is.na(x$subj))) sprintf("partial (%.0f%% subject-labelled)",
                                         100 * mean(!is.na(x$subj)))
    else "subject-resolved"
  out
}
# Sample-size gate: a level needs >= 5 units to enter, and >= 2 levels must
# survive.
gate <- function(a, min_level = 5) {
  a <- a[a$g %in% names(table(a$g))[table(a$g) >= min_level], ]
  if (dplyr::n_distinct(a$g) < 2) NULL else a
}
# >= 3 events AND >= 3 non-events, or the table degenerates and Fisher is
# undefined.
fish <- function(g, v) if (sum(v) >= 3 && sum(!v) >= 3)
  fisher.test(table(g, v), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 20000)$p.value else NA_real_
```

```{r unit-design-table}
design_tbl <- pm |>
  dplyr::group_by(study) |>
  dplyr::summarise(files = dplyr::n(),
                   subjects = dplyr::n_distinct(subj[!is.na(subj)]),
                   subject_recorded = paste0(round(100 * mean(!is.na(subj))), "%"),
                   files_per_subject = ifelse(dplyr::n_distinct(subj[!is.na(subj)]) > 0,
                     round(dplyr::n() / dplyr::n_distinct(subj[!is.na(subj)]), 1), NA),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(dplyr::coalesce(files_per_subject, 0)))
knitr::kable(design_tbl, caption = "Study designs: how many files stand behind one person")
```

Read the top and bottom rows. The probe cohort is
`r design_tbl$files_per_subject[1]` files per subject, so any test run on its
raw rows is inflated roughly that many times over. The three deposits reporting
`0` subjects record no subject identifier at all, so nothing there can be
de-duplicated and every contrast in them is exploratory.

## What propagation unlocks: a per-dataset contrast scan

The question this section answers is not "does propagation find more files" but
**"does propagation let a single deposit answer a question it otherwise could
not"**. That is a per-dataset question, tested inside each deposit, with no
pooling anywhere.

Every combination of study, stratifier and compound is tested twice: once using
only the MASST MS2 detections, once using the MS1-propagated detections. A
contrast enters only if it clears the sample-size gate above. Because this is a
scan of several dozen contrasts, both methods get Benjamini-Hochberg control
across everything they can test.

```{r unlock-scan}
STRAT <- c(sex = "sex2", `body site` = "site",
           `clinical group` = "clin", `age band` = "ageb")
ROLES <- list(omeprazole        = c("par_ms2", "par_ms1"),
              `5-OH-omeprazole` = c("met_ms2", "met_ms1"),
              `either compound` = c("ms2", "ms1"))
set.seed(1)
scan_rows <- list()
for (s in unique(pm$study)) for (vn in names(STRAT)) for (rn in names(ROLES)) {
  x  <- pm[pm$study == s, , drop = FALSE]
  a0 <- units_for(x, x[[STRAT[[vn]]]], ROLES[[rn]])
  if (is.null(a0)) next
  dsg <- attr(a0, "design"); a <- gate(a0)
  if (is.null(a)) next
  p2 <- fish(a$g, a[[ROLES[[rn]][1]]]); p1 <- fish(a$g, a[[ROLES[[rn]][2]]])
  if (is.na(p1) && is.na(p2)) next
  scan_rows[[length(scan_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    study = s, stratifier = vn, compound = rn, design = dsg, units = nrow(a),
    det_ms2 = sum(a[[ROLES[[rn]][1]]]), det_ms1 = sum(a[[ROLES[[rn]][2]]]),
    p2 = p2, p1 = p1)
}
SCAN <- dplyr::bind_rows(scan_rows)
SCAN$q2 <- NA_real_; SCAN$q1 <- NA_real_
SCAN$q2[!is.na(SCAN$p2)] <- p.adjust(SCAN$p2[!is.na(SCAN$p2)], "BH")
SCAN$q1[!is.na(SCAN$p1)] <- p.adjust(SCAN$p1[!is.na(SCAN$p1)], "BH")

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  method = c("MASST MS2 only", "MS1 propagated"),
  testable = c(sum(!is.na(SCAN$p2)), sum(!is.na(SCAN$p1))),
  significant_FDR_05 = c(sum(SCAN$q2 < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                         sum(SCAN$q1 < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))),
  caption = "Contrasts each method can test, and how many survive FDR control")
```

```{r unlock-table}
sig <- SCAN[!is.na(SCAN$q1) & SCAN$q1 < 0.05, ]
sig <- sig[order(sig$q1), ]
sig$MASST <- ifelse(is.na(sig$q2), "could not test",
             ifelse(sig$q2 < 0.05, sprintf("also found it (q = %.3g)", sig$q2),
                    sprintf("NOT significant (q = %.3g)", sig$q2)))
sig$new <- is.na(sig$q2) | sig$q2 >= 0.05
knitr::kable(sig |> dplyr::transmute(study, stratifier, compound, design, units,
                                     MS2 = det_ms2, MS1 = det_ms1, MASST,
                                     q_MS1 = sprintf("%.3g", q1)),
             caption = "Every contrast MS1 finds at FDR 0.05, and what MASST said about it")

lost <- SCAN[!is.na(SCAN$q2) & SCAN$q2 < 0.05 & (is.na(SCAN$q1) | SCAN$q1 >= 0.05), ]
```

```{r fig-unlock-scan, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
#| echo: false
.s <- sig
.s$label <- paste0(.s$study, "\n", .s$stratifier, ", ", .s$compound)
.s$label <- factor(.s$label, levels = rev(.s$label))
.pl <- tidyr::pivot_longer(.s[, c("label", "design", "q2", "q1")],
                           c(q2, q1), names_to = "method", values_to = "q")
.pl$method <- ifelse(.pl$method == "q1", "MS1 propagated", "MASST MS2 only")
.pl$q[is.na(.pl$q)] <- 1.2                       # "could not test" parked off-scale
ggplot(.pl, aes(q, label, colour = method, shape = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(aes(group = label), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10",
                     breaks = c(1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 0.05, 0.2, 1),
                     labels = c("0.0001", "0.001", "0.01", "0.05", "0.2", "1 / n.t.")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("MS1 propagated" = "#111111",
                                 "MASST MS2 only" = "#9a9a9a"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("MS1 propagated" = 16, "MASST MS2 only" = 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Benjamini-Hochberg q, log scale", y = NULL,
       title = "Benjamini-Hochberg q per within-deposit contrast, MASST MS2 and MS1-propagated") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5, lineheight = 0.95),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5))
```

Three numbers matter here.

**Nothing is lost.** `r nrow(lost)` contrasts that MASST finds significant fail
to replicate under propagation. Whatever else propagation does, it does not
overturn the MS2 result, which is the minimum a match-between-runs method has to
demonstrate.

**`r sum(sig$new)` of `r nrow(sig)` findings are new**: MASST either could not
test the contrast at all or returned a null. Of those,
**`r sum(sig$new & sig$design == "subject-resolved")` sit on a subject-resolved
design** and are the ones worth quoting; the remainder are in deposits with no
subject identifier and are exploratory.

**The defensible new findings are all the same finding.** They are the
COVID-severity contrasts in MTBLS1866 and MTBLS11656, which is to say the two
cohorts that also replicate each other in the section above. The per-dataset
scan and the replication are the same fact approached from two directions, which
is the strongest form the evidence takes anywhere in this project.

MTBLS1866 is the demonstration piece. On the MASST detections the
metabolite-versus- severity contrast returns a **perfect null**: three detected
subjects, q = 1. MS1 supplies 37 and the same contrast in the same cohort
becomes q = 0.0003. Nothing about the cohort, the metadata or the test changed.
Only whether the compound was looked for in MS1.

Two cautions, both visible in the table. The body-site contrasts in MSV000094097
look strong and cannot be claimed, because that deposit records no subjects and
its 144 files might be 144 people or 36 people sampled at four sites. And the
probe cohort's body-site contrasts are significant under **both** methods once
aggregated to 55 subject-by-site units; on raw files they were computed across
1,125 rows from 14 people, which was never a valid test even though it happened
to reach the same verdict.

### The one deposit worth showing despite an unknown design

MSV000094097 produces the largest single jump in the scan and cannot be counted
as a result, so it is worth showing exactly as it is rather than dropping it.
MASST finds the metabolite in 2 of its files. Propagation finds it in 32, across
four body sites, and the body-site contrast goes from untestable to q = 0.0003.

```{r fig-094097, fig.width = 7.6, fig.height = 4.2}
#| echo: false

.t97 <- .d97 |>
  dplyr::group_by(site) |>
  dplyr::summarise(files = dplyr::n(),
                   `omeprazole (MS2)` = sum(par_ms2), `omeprazole (MS1)` = sum(par_ms1),
                   `5-OH-omeprazole (MS2)` = sum(met_ms2), `5-OH-omeprazole (MS1)` = sum(met_ms1),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(site, files), names_to = "panel", values_to = "count") |>
  tidyr::separate(panel, into = c("compound", "method"), sep = " \\(") |>
  dplyr::mutate(method = sub("\\)", "", method), rate = count / files,
                col = factor(paste0(compound, "\n", method),
                             levels = c("omeprazole\nMS2", "omeprazole\nMS1",
                                        "5-OH-omeprazole\nMS2", "5-OH-omeprazole\nMS1")),
                row = paste0(site, "  (", files, " files)"))
ggplot(.t97, aes(col, reorder(row, rate, sum), fill = rate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = count, colour = rate > 0.3), size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey15"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey94", high = "black", guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Files with a detection by body site, MSV000094097") +
```
