
The pattern is the one the rest of the corpus shows: both compounds present in
the blood fractions, the metabolite reaching further than the parent, and the
non-blood sites near empty. That coherence is why it is worth showing. What
cannot be done is attach a p-value to it, because without subject identifiers
there is no way to know whether the four body sites are four samples from the
same person, in which case the contrast is paired and the test is invalid.

This is a **metadata** limitation, not a measurement one. The spectra are fine;
the deposit simply never recorded who each file came from. It is the single
clearest argument in this project for depositors recording a subject identifier.

## The corpus-wide gain, with and without the metadata restriction

The per-cohort table above counts only files a metadata source covers, because
every stratified analysis downstream needs that metadata. But the pipeline
extracts from more files than that: a file with no metadata still yields a valid
presence call, it just cannot be assigned to a subject or a group. Both numbers
are worth stating, because they answer different questions. The unrestricted row
is what the extraction actually recovers; the restricted row is what survives
into an analysis.

```{r prevalence-gain-total}
#| echo: false
# DUP_STUDY / dup_key as defined with the MS2 baseline above; the reasoning for
# why only this pair collapses, and why 092754/092757 must not, is stated there.

prop_totals <- function(d, label, dedup_files = TRUE) {
  d$fk <- fkey(d$file)
  dk   <- unique(paste0(d$dataset_id, "|", d$fk))
  mh   <- masst_hits[masst_hits$dk %in% dk, ]
  if (dedup_files) {
    # Count distinct physical files per role. dup_key must not be deduplicated
    # across roles first: a file with both a parent and a metabolite hit would
    # collapse to one row and silently drop a role (this deflated the metabolite
    # MS2 baseline 526 -> 146 and inflated its gain to 8x). Dedup within each
    # role.
    d  <- d[!duplicated(dup_key(d$dataset_id, d$fk)), ]
    nd <- function(role) {
      r <- mh[mh$role == role, ]
      length(unique(dup_key(r$dataset_id, r$fk)))
    }
  } else {
    nd <- function(role) nrow(dplyr::distinct(mh[mh$role == role, c("dataset_id", "fk")]))
  }
  p2 <- nd("parent"); m2 <- nd("metabolite")
  p1 <- sum(d$detection_tier %in% c("both", "parent_only"))
  m1 <- sum(d$detection_tier %in% c("both", "metab_only"))
  fmt <- function(ms2, ms1) if (ms2 > 0)
    sprintf("%d -> %d  (%.1fx)", ms2, ms1, ms1 / ms2) else
    sprintf("%d -> %d  (n/a)", ms2, ms1)
  data.frame(
    scope                    = label,
    files                    = nrow(d),
    `omeprazole: MS2 -> MS1` = fmt(p2, p1),
    `5-OH: MS2 -> MS1`       = fmt(m2, m1),
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
rbind(
  prop_totals(samples_perfile, "all extracted, DISTINCT files",   dedup_files = TRUE),
  prop_totals(pf,              "metadata-carrying, DISTINCT",     dedup_files = TRUE),
  prop_totals(samples_perfile, "all extracted, summed (INFLATED)", dedup_files = FALSE))
```

The MS2 baseline here is **every MASST hit in `hits_curated`**, not just the
subset we sent to SIRIUS. That matters: the confirmation step was capped per
role per dataset, so dividing by the confirmed count would measure our own cap
rather than the method, and inflates the gain several-fold. The uncapped
baseline is the conservative choice and the one a "classic" MS2-only reanalysis
would have had.

## What the spread across cohorts tells us

The spread of detection rate across cohorts is not noise; it is the biology of
who is exposed. Two regimes are visible:

- **Drug-probe cohorts** (every subject dosed by design) sit near 100% for both
  compounds. They are the internal positive control: propagation should, and
  does, recover almost everything there.
- **General-population and disease cohorts** sit low, because only incidentally
  dosed subjects carry the drug. Here the MS1-over-MS2 gain is largest, and the
  absolute number of recovered exposures is the payoff: a few percent of a large
  cohort is still tens of subjects the MS2-only analysis would have missed.

The metabolite frequently has a higher detection rate than the parent (e.g. in
excretory matrices), which is expected pharmacology, not an artefact: omeprazole
is extensively metabolised, so in urine or feces the metabolite persists while
the parent is largely gone. This asymmetry is itself a hypothesis-generating
readout and is exactly the kind of pattern the presence analysis surfaces.

## Does a cohort finding replicate in an independent cohort?

The strongest argument for assembling a corpus rather than analysing one deposit
is that a claim can be **tested twice, in populations that share nothing**. Two
deposits here stratify subjects by COVID-19 severity and were produced by
unrelated groups on different continents: MTBLS1866 (Italy) and MTBLS11656
(China). Neither was collected to study omeprazole, and neither knows about the
other. If severity really tracks exposure, the pattern should appear in both.

Note this pairing is the opposite situation to MSV000082493 / MSV000084008
below, which look like two cohorts but are one study re-deposited twice.
Replication requires independence, so establishing it is a prerequisite for
reading anything as a second observation rather than an echo of the first.

```{r severity-replication}
rep_sets <- c(MTBLS1866 = "Italy", MTBLS11656 = "China")

# A column that is empty for every row is read as logical NA, and nzchar(NA) is
# TRUE, so the "is this column populated" test must exclude NA or it always
# passes.
filled <- function(v) !is.na(v) & nzchar(as.character(v))

rep_rows <- lapply(names(rep_sets), function(acc) {
  x <- pf[grepl(paste0("^", acc, "(_|$)"), pf$dataset_id), , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(x)) return(NULL)
  # Deposits differ in which column carries the severity strata; take whichever
  # one this deposit actually populates.
  g  <- if (sum(filled(x$health_status)) > 10) x$health_status else x$group
  ok <- filled(g)
  data.frame(cohort = paste0(acc, " (", rep_sets[[acc]], ")"),
             stratum = as.character(g)[ok],
             par = x$detection_tier[ok] %in% c("both", "parent_only"),
             met = x$detection_tier[ok] %in% c("both", "metab_only"),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
rep_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(rep_rows)

rep_tbl <- rep_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(cohort, stratum) |>
  dplyr::summarise(files = dplyr::n(),
                   omeprazole = sum(par), `5-OH` = sum(met), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(cohort, dplyr::desc(`5-OH` / files))

B_SIM <- 20000
set.seed(1)   # the p is simulated, so pin it or the reported value drifts per render
# A simulated Fisher p cannot go below 1/(B+1). Printing that floor as "0.0000"
# would claim a precision the simulation does not have, so show it as an upper
# bound.
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p <= 1 / (B_SIM + 1),
                            sprintf("< %.0e", 1 / (B_SIM + 1)), sprintf("%.4f", p))

rep_p <- rep_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(cohort) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p_parent = fmt_p(fisher.test(table(stratum, par),
                                 simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = B_SIM)$p.value),
    p_metabolite = fmt_p(fisher.test(table(stratum, met),
                                     simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = B_SIM)$p.value),
    .groups = "drop")

knitr::kable(rep_tbl, caption = "Detected files per severity stratum, two independent cohorts")
knitr::kable(rep_p,
             caption = "Fisher exact test of stratum against detection, within each cohort")
```

```{r fig-replication, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.4}
#| echo: false
.rl <- rep_tbl |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(omeprazole, `5-OH`), names_to = "compound", values_to = "detected") |>
  dplyr::mutate(stratum = paste0(stratum, "  (n=", files, ")"),
                compound = factor(ifelse(compound == "5-OH", "5-OH-omeprazole", "omeprazole"),
                                  levels = c("omeprazole", "5-OH-omeprazole")))
ggplot(.rl, aes(reorder(stratum, detected), detected, fill = compound)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.72), width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = detected), position = position_dodge(width = 0.72),
            hjust = -0.35, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() + facet_wrap(~ cohort, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(omeprazole = "#1b1b1b", `5-OH-omeprazole` = "#9a9a9a"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.16))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "files with the compound detected",
       title = "Files with a detection by COVID-19 severity stratum, two independent cohorts") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey93", colour = NA),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5))
```

Both cohorts give the same ordering, and in both the **healthy control stratum
contributes zero detected files of either compound**. That the healthy groups
are exactly empty in two unrelated populations is the part that a single deposit
cannot establish: within one cohort an empty control group is a plausible
accident of size, whereas twice it is the negative control the corpus was
assembled to provide.

The reading is exposure, not pathology. Omeprazole is prescribed heavily in
hospital and intensive care, so what replicates is that the sicker strata are
the medicated strata. The finding is that the pipeline recovers a real,
interpretable prescribing gradient from data deposited for an unrelated purpose,
in two countries at once.

### Does the exposure reading hold up everywhere it can be checked?

Calling these associations exposure rather than pathology is not a hedge, it is
a testable claim: if the pipeline is measuring who was **prescribed**
omeprazole, then the drug should concentrate in strata receiving more medical
care, and should be near absent where none is given. Crucially it should track
*care*, not illness as such, so a cohort stratified by a disease that does not
change prescribing should show nothing. Four independent studies record a
clinical grouping and can be checked.

```{r fig-exposure-sense, fig.width = 8.4, fig.height = 5.4}
#| echo: false
.cl <- pm |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(clin), nzchar(clin))
.cl$unit <- ifelse(is.na(.cl$subj), paste(.cl$study, .cl$fk),
                   paste(.cl$study, .cl$subj, .cl$clin))
.cs <- .cl |>
  dplyr::group_by(unit) |>
  dplyr::summarise(study = dplyr::first(study), clin = dplyr::first(clin),
                   ms1 = any(ms1), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::group_by(study, clin) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), det = sum(ms1), rate = mean(ms1), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::group_by(study) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() >= 2, sum(n) >= 20) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
.cs$label <- paste0(.cs$clin, "  (", .cs$n, ")")
ggplot(.cs, aes(rate, reorder(label, rate))) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = "grey25") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d/%d", det, n)), hjust = -0.18, size = 3.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ study, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.22))) +
  labs(x = "subjects with a detection", y = NULL,
       title = "Subjects with a detection by clinical stratum, per study") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey93", colour = NA),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5))
```

The gradient is **not** uniform across the four, and that is the informative
part.

It is strong in exactly the two cohorts whose strata differ in **intensity of
hospital care**: MTBLS1866 runs from 78% in patients who survived intensive care
down to 0 of 26 healthy, and MTBLS11656 from severe disease down to 0 of 45 in
both the mild and the healthy arms. It is absent in the Chagas cohort, where the
strata are infection status in what is largely an outpatient population, and
where infected (11 of 72) and healthy (1 of 6) sit at the same rate. ST002722
has 6 subjects in its second arm and cannot say anything either way.

That pattern is what makes the exposure reading credible rather than convenient.
If the pipeline were picking up something generic about being unwell, Chagas
infection should have moved it too. It does not, because Chagas outpatients are
not receiving stress-ulcer prophylaxis, whereas intensive-care patients very
often are. The signal tracks **care intensity, not illness**, which is precisely
what a prescribing signal should do and what a disease-mechanism signal should
not.

Stating it as exposure is therefore a **strength of the result, not a caveat on
it**. It would be far more worrying to find omeprazole distributed at random
across clinical strata, or concentrated in the healthy arms. The claim is that
the readout works, and this is the evidence that it does; the claim is not that
COVID-19 causes omeprazole to appear in plasma.

## Pooling presence across studies: a random-effects meta-analysis

The scan above asks what each deposit can answer on its own. This asks the
stronger question: measure a contrast **inside** each study, then pool the
study-level effects. Nothing crosses a study boundary except a log odds ratio,
so the response-factor offset and the isomer are both irrelevant, and
between-study disagreement becomes a measured quantity (`I2`) instead of an
assumption.

The unit is the one defined above: one subject per contrast level, with deposits
that record no subject flagged rather than silently treated as independent.
Because the same question can be put to the MS2 baseline, this is also the
sharpest available test of what propagation buys at the corpus level.

```{r pool-helpers}
# DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling of log odds ratios.
dl_pool <- function(yi, vi) {
  wf <- 1 / vi; mf <- sum(wf * yi) / sum(wf)
  Q  <- sum(wf * (yi - mf)^2); df <- length(yi) - 1
  C  <- sum(wf) - sum(wf^2) / sum(wf)
  tau2 <- max(0, (Q - df) / C)
  w <- 1 / (vi + tau2); m <- sum(w * yi) / sum(w); se <- sqrt(1 / sum(w))
  list(OR = exp(m), lo = exp(m - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(m + 1.96 * se),
       p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(m / se)), I2 = max(0, 100 * (Q - df) / Q), k = length(yi))
}
# Haldane 0.5 correction only when a cell is empty, which it often is here.
or_2x2 <- function(grp, det) {
  a <- sum(grp & det); b <- sum(grp & !det); c <- sum(!grp & det); e <- sum(!grp & !det)
  if (min(a, b, c, e) == 0) { a <- a + .5; b <- b + .5; c <- c + .5; e <- e + .5 }
  c(yi = log((a * e) / (b * c)), vi = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/e)
}
fmt_pool <- function(p) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f), p = %.3g, I2 = %.0f%%, k = %d",
                                p$OR, p$lo, p$hi, p$p, p$I2, p$k)
```

### The unexposed-by-design stratum

Three studies contain a stratum that should carry no drug: the healthy arms of
the two COVID cohorts, and the uninfected arm of the Chagas serum study. Each
study's reference level is taken from **its own vocabulary**, never from a name
match, which would otherwise sweep in QC and blank injections and invert the
result.

```{r pool-reference}
# The Chagas deposit carries TWO unexposed labels, "uninfected" and "healthy",
# as separate strata. Taking only one of them would be a choice made after
# seeing the answer, so both are used. It is also the conservative direction:
# the "healthy" arm contains the single detection, which weakens the contrast
# rather than helping it.
REF <- list("MTBLS1866"    = "non-COVID-19 healthy",
            "MTBLS11656"   = "Healthy Control",
            "Chagas serum" = c("uninfected", "healthy"))

ref_rows <- function(role) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(REF), function(s) {
    x  <- pm[pm$study == s, , drop = FALSE]
    a  <- units_for(x, x$clin, role)
    if (is.null(a)) return(NULL)
    ref <- a$g %in% REF[[s]]
    if (sum(ref) < 5 || sum(!ref) < 5) return(NULL)
    o <- or_2x2(ref, a[[role]])
    data.frame(study = s, reference = paste(REF[[s]], collapse = " + "),
               ref_units = sum(ref), ref_detected = sum(ref & a[[role]]),
               other_units = sum(!ref), other_detected = sum(!ref & a[[role]]),
               yi = o[["yi"]], vi = o[["vi"]])
  }))
}
ref_ms1 <- ref_rows("ms1"); ref_ms2 <- ref_rows("ms2")
pr1 <- dl_pool(ref_ms1$yi, ref_ms1$vi); pr2 <- dl_pool(ref_ms2$yi, ref_ms2$vi)

knitr::kable(ref_ms1[, 1:6],
             caption = "Detections in the unexposed-by-design stratum, per subject")
knitr::kable(data.frame(method = c("MASST MS2 only", "MS1 propagated"),
                        pooled_OR = c(fmt_pool(pr2), fmt_pool(pr1))),
             caption = "Pooled odds of detection in the reference stratum versus the rest")
```

**`r sum(ref_ms1$ref_detected)` detection in `r sum(ref_ms1$ref_units)`
reference subjects across three independent studies**, against
`r sum(ref_ms1$other_detected)` in the rest, with `I2 = 0%`. The two COVID
cohorts contribute exact zeros; the single detection is in the Chagas healthy
arm, which is one subject of six and is exactly the kind of incidental
prescription a general-population arm is expected to contain.

The MS2 row is the point. On the MASST baseline the same three studies pool to p
= `r sprintf("%.3f", pr2$p)`, which clears no threshold. **The contrast becomes
significant only once propagation supplies the detections** (p =
`r sprintf("%.4f", pr1$p)`), and it does so without putting a single false
positive into the strata where the drug should be absent. This is the
corpus-level analogue of the pre-dose negative control in `04`.

### Sex: does propagation move an estimate, or only sharpen it?

Sex is the one variable testable in five independent studies under **both**
methods, which makes it the place to ask whether adding propagated detections
biases a pooled effect rather than merely narrowing it.

```{r pool-sex}
sex_pool <- function(role) {
  tb <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(unique(pm$study), function(s) {
    x <- pm[pm$study == s, , drop = FALSE]
    a <- units_for(x, x$sex2, role); if (is.null(a)) return(NULL)
    a <- gate(a); if (is.null(a)) return(NULL)
    if (sum(a[[role]]) < 3 || sum(!a[[role]]) < 3) return(NULL)
    o <- or_2x2(a$g == "female", a[[role]])
    data.frame(study = s, design = attr(units_for(x, x$sex2, role), "design"),
               units = nrow(a), detected = sum(a[[role]]),
               yi = o[["yi"]], vi = o[["vi"]])
  }))
  if (nrow(tb) < 2) return(NULL)
  list(tb = tb, p = dl_pool(tb$yi, tb$vi))
}
sx2 <- sex_pool("ms2"); sx1 <- sex_pool("ms1")
knitr::kable(sx1$tb[, c("study", "design", "units", "detected")],
             caption = "Studies contributing to the sex contrast, per subject")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  method = c("MASST MS2 only", "MS1 propagated"),
  pooled_OR_female_vs_male = c(fmt_pool(sx2$p), fmt_pool(sx1$p)),
  CI_width_log_odds = round(c(log(sx2$p$hi) - log(sx2$p$lo),
                              log(sx1$p$hi) - log(sx1$p$lo)), 2)),
  caption = "Sex contrast pooled over five independent studies under each method")
```

Both are null and both have `I2 = 0%`, so propagation does not manufacture an
association. What it changes is precision: the interval narrows from
`r sprintf("%.2f", log(sx2$p$hi) - log(sx2$p$lo))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", log(sx1$p$hi) - log(sx1$p$lo))` log-odds, which turns an
interval spanning roughly a `r sprintf("%.0f", sx2$p$hi / sx2$p$lo)`-fold range,
and therefore compatible with almost anything, into a usefully bounded null.

This is the check a match-between-runs method owes before its extra detections
are trusted in any association analysis, and it is only possible because sex
happens to be recorded in five studies. It is not itself a biological result.

### Age: where propagation prevents a claim rather than enabling one

```{r pool-age}
age_pool <- function(role) {
  tb <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(unique(pm$study), function(s) {
    x <- pm[pm$study == s & is.finite(pm$agen), , drop = FALSE]
    if (!nrow(x)) return(NULL)
    # Collapse to people where the deposit supports it; where it records no
    # subject, the file is the unit and the estimate is labelled as resting on
    # an unknown design.
    known <- subject_resolved(x$subj, sibling_ids = unlist(sibling_id_map[unique(x$dataset_id)], use.names = FALSE))
    a <- data.frame(u = if (known) x$subj else x$fk, agen = x$agen, y = x[[role]]) |>
      dplyr::group_by(u) |>
      dplyr::summarise(agen = dplyr::first(agen), y = any(y), .groups = "drop")
    if (nrow(a) < 20 || sum(a$y) < 5 || sum(!a$y) < 5) return(NULL)
    if (diff(range(a$agen)) < 10) return(NULL)
    m <- try(glm(y ~ I(agen / 10), data = a, family = binomial))
    if (inherits(m, "try-error")) return(NULL)
    co <- summary(m)$coefficients
    if (!"I(agen/10)" %in% rownames(co)) return(NULL)
    data.frame(study = s, design = if (known) "subject-resolved" else "design unknown",
               subjects = nrow(a),
               age_range = paste0(round(min(a$agen)), " to ", round(max(a$agen))),
               OR_per_decade = round(exp(co["I(agen/10)", "Estimate"]), 2),
               yi = co["I(agen/10)", "Estimate"], vi = co["I(agen/10)", "Std. Error"]^2)
  }))
  if (nrow(tb) < 2) return(NULL)
  list(tb = tb, p = dl_pool(tb$yi, tb$vi))
}
ag2 <- age_pool("ms2"); ag1 <- age_pool("ms1")
knitr::kable(ag1$tb[, c("study", "design", "subjects", "age_range", "OR_per_decade")],
             caption = "The age slopes, with the cohorts that produced them")
knitr::kable(data.frame(method = c("MASST MS2 only", "MS1 propagated"),
                        pooled_OR_per_decade = c(fmt_pool(ag2$p), fmt_pool(ag1$p))),
             caption = "Detection against age, logistic within each study then pooled")
```

```{r fig-pooled-forest, fig.width = 8.6, fig.height = 4.4}
#| echo: false
.row <- function(p, contrast, method) data.frame(
  contrast = contrast, method = method, OR = p$OR, lo = p$lo, hi = p$hi,
  note = sprintf("k=%d  I2=%.0f%%  p=%s", p$k, p$I2,
                 ifelse(p$p < 0.001, format(signif(p$p, 1), scientific = TRUE),
                        format(round(p$p, 3), nsmall = 3))))
.f <- rbind(
  .row(pr2, "Unexposed stratum\nvs the rest", "MASST MS2 only"),
  .row(pr1, "Unexposed stratum\nvs the rest", "MS1 propagated"),
  .row(sx2$p, "Female vs male", "MASST MS2 only"),
  .row(sx1$p, "Female vs male", "MS1 propagated"),
  .row(ag2$p, "Per decade of age", "MASST MS2 only"),
  .row(ag1$p, "Per decade of age", "MS1 propagated"))
.f$contrast <- factor(.f$contrast, levels = rev(unique(.f$contrast)))
ggplot(.f, aes(OR, contrast, colour = method, shape = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.16,
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.62), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.62)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = note), position = position_dodge(width = 0.62),
            hjust = 0, vjust = -1.1, size = 2.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10", breaks = c(0.02, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("MS1 propagated" = "#111111",
                                 "MASST MS2 only" = "#9a9a9a"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("MS1 propagated" = 16, "MASST MS2 only" = 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "pooled odds ratio (log scale), random effects", y = NULL,
       title = "Random-effects pooled odds ratio per contrast, MASST MS2 and MS1-propagated") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5))
```

Read this one carefully, because the naive version is wrong. Restricted to the
MASST detections only **`r ag2$p$k` studies** can fit an age term
(`r paste(ag2$tb$study, collapse = " and ")`, `r sum(ag2$tb$subjects)` units
between them), they happen to agree, and the pool returns a significant
`r sprintf("%.2f", ag2$p$OR)`-fold increase per decade, which flatters a
well-known prescribing pattern. Propagation lets **`r ag1$p$k` studies** fit it
and the pooled effect collapses to non-significance with `I2 =
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", ag1$p$I2)``.

**At `r ag2$p$k` studies, `I2` cannot detect heterogeneity at all.** The MS2
answer is not cleaner than the MS1 answer; it is blind. That is the clearest
statement in this notebook of what an MS2-only corpus analysis costs: not merely
fewer detections, but too few studies to see that the studies disagree.

#### Why they disagree, and why pooling harder cannot fix it

The heterogeneity is structural. **Every study that can fit a slope is a
clinical cohort**, and age inside a hospital population is a proxy for case-mix:
a Chagas infection cohort, a spot-urine cohort from a Glasgow clinic, a cohort
of older adults with chronic illness. Each slope measures who in *that*
population was prescribed a proton-pump inhibitor, which is a different quantity
in each. And the **age ranges barely overlap**, as the table shows: a per-decade
linear slope fitted to a cohort spanning the thirties and one fitted to a cohort
spanning the sixties describe different segments of a relationship there is no
reason to think is linear. They were never estimating a common parameter, so the
pooling was ill-posed before the data arrived.

#### The clean version of the question cannot be asked here

The way to remove the case-mix confound is to ask only about people who are not
patients. The corpus does not support it.

```{r pool-age-healthy}
HEALTHY <- list("MTBLS1866"      = "non-COVID-19 healthy",
                "MTBLS11656"     = "Healthy Control",
                "Chagas serum"   = "uninfected",
                "MSV000082433"   = "healthy",
                "MSV000091520"   = "healthy",
                "Jarmusch probe" = "healthy")
healthy_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(HEALTHY), function(s) {
  x <- pm[pm$study == s, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(x)) return(NULL)
  v <- nz(x$health_status)
  h <- !is.na(v) & tolower(v) == tolower(HEALTHY[[s]])
  if (!any(h)) return(NULL)
  y <- x[h, , drop = FALSE]
  u <- if (!all(is.na(y$subj))) dplyr::n_distinct(y$subj) else nrow(y)
  data.frame(study = s, healthy_units = u,
             age = if (all(is.na(y$agen))) "not recorded" else
                   paste0(round(min(y$agen, na.rm = TRUE)), " to ",
                          round(max(y$agen, na.rm = TRUE))),
             MS1_detected = sum(y$ms1), MS2_detected = sum(y$ms2))
}))
knitr::kable(healthy_tbl, caption = "Healthy strata: do any have age and events together?")
```

Six studies carry a healthy stratum. Three record no age at all. Of those that
do, two contribute almost no events, and the probe cohort's detections exist
only because every subject was **dosed by design**, which answers a different
question and records no age anyway. That leaves roughly nine detections in
healthy people with a recorded age, and five of those are MSV000082433's, which
the closing subsection shows are metabolite-without-parent in non-blood sites
and most likely the isomer.

The negative is worth stating positively: **background exposure in non-clinical
populations is close to zero here**, which converges with the unexposed-stratum
result above and is precisely why age is unaskable. Omeprazole in this corpus
marks clinical care, so any age effect is inseparable from the setting that
produced it. We report no pooled age association.

### What does not pool

- **Body site.** Only one study has two body sites with enough subjects, so the
  biofluid view below is a pooled description and not a meta-analysis.
- **MSV000082433.** It contributes five MS1 detections MASST does not have, but
  all five are **metabolite without parent**, in five different non-blood sites
  (nasal cavity, vagina, oral cavity, arm skin), in healthy women aged 18 to 33.
  That is the signature of the isobaric interference described in `03`, not of
  drug exposure, and the deposit is not counted as a propagation success
  anywhere here.

## Prevalence by biofluid: the reverse-metabolomics biology view

The heatmap above is organised by cohort to show the method's value (MS2 vs
MS1). The reverse-metabolomics papers instead organise prevalence by a **biology
axis** (tissue / biofluid / health phenotype); Gentry et al. (Nature 2024, Fig
2b-d) is the canonical example, a molecule-by-tissue and
molecule-by-health-condition prevalence heatmap. We reproduce that view here,
MS1-propagated: pooling across cohorts by body site, the detection prevalence of
each compound.

Since this is a cross-repository comparison it is computed **per specimen**, on
the same collapsed table the meta-analysis above uses. A file-level version
would let the probe cohort's replicate injections dominate the plasma row simply
by having been injected more often, which is a property of its protocol rather
than of plasma.

This pooling deliberately crosses cohorts, so exposure and body site are partly
confounded (a biofluid seen only in a drug-probe cohort will read high for
reasons of study design, not physiology). It is therefore hypothesis-generating,
in exactly the spirit the field uses it: the expected signal is that the parent
concentrates in blood/plasma while the metabolite persists in excretory matrices
(urine, feces), which if it appears is the pharmacology falling out of public
data with no targeted assay.

```{r prevalence-by-biofluid, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5}
# Same unit rule as everywhere else, built explicitly here because this table
# also needs the study, to show how many cohorts stand behind each matrix.
bysite <- pm |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(site)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(.u = ifelse(is.na(subj), paste(study, fk), paste(study, subj, site))) |>
  dplyr::group_by(.u) |>
  dplyr::summarise(site = dplyr::first(site), study = dplyr::first(study),
                   par_ms1 = any(par_ms1), met_ms1 = any(met_ms1), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::group_by(site) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_specimens = dplyr::n(),
                   n_studies = dplyr::n_distinct(study),
                   omeprazole = mean(par_ms1), `5-OH-omeprazole` = mean(met_ms1),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::filter(n_specimens >= 5) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(omeprazole, `5-OH-omeprazole`),
                      names_to = "compound", values_to = "rate")

ggplot(bysite, aes(x = compound,
                   y = reorder(paste0(site, "  (", n_specimens, " specimens, ",
                                      n_studies, ifelse(n_studies == 1, " study)", " studies)")),
                                rate, sum),
                   fill = rate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 1),
                colour = rate > 0.45), size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey15"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "#762a83",
                      labels = scales::percent, name = "MS1 detection\nrate") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "MS1-propagated detection prevalence by body site, per specimen") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The study count on each row is the part to read first. A body site carried by
one study is that study's exposure pattern wearing a biofluid label, and only
the rows backed by several cohorts describe anything about the matrix itself.

## The ratio across cohorts: measuring the offset instead of assuming it

Prevalence is a per-compound presence question, and presence rests on the
parent, which has no isobaric twin. The parent/metabolite **ratio** is a
different kind of object: a quantity whose absolute value carries a per-method
response-factor offset. The standing position in this project has been that the
offset is unknown, so ratios must not be pooled across cohorts. That position is
defensible but untested, and the corpus turns out to contain the experiment that
tests it.

### Trying to measure the offset directly, and failing to pin it down

MSV000092754 and MSV000092757 are the **same subjects and the same serum**, run
on HILIC and on reverse phase. Biology is held constant by construction, so
whatever separates the two deposits is method. This is the only place in the
corpus where the offset can be observed rather than assumed, so it is worth
asking what it gives.

```{r ratio-offset}
ratio_pf <- pf |>
  dplyr::filter(detection_tier == "both", is.finite(log2_ratio))

# One study under two accessions must not count twice; two accessions of one
# subject panel on two columns must not be merged. Both rules are established
# above.
ratio_pf$study <- dplyr::case_when(
  grepl(paste(DUP_STUDY, collapse = "|"), ratio_pf$dataset_id) ~ "Jarmusch probe (082493 + 084008)",
  grepl("MSV000092754|MSV000092757", ratio_pf$dataset_id)      ~ "Chagas serum (092754 + 092757)",
  TRUE ~ short_ds(ratio_pf$dataset_id))

chagas <- ratio_pf |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("MSV000092754|MSV000092757", dataset_id)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(chromatography = ifelse(grepl("092754", dataset_id), "HILIC", "RP"))

chagas_grp <- chagas |>
  dplyr::group_by(chromatography) |>
  dplyr::summarise(files = dplyr::n(), subjects = dplyr::n_distinct(subject_id),
                   median_log2 = median(log2_ratio), .groups = "drop")
OFFSET_GRP <- abs(diff(chagas_grp$median_log2))

# The paired form is the design that actually holds biology fixed: the same
# person on both columns. It is also far smaller, because few subjects yield a
# ratio twice.
chagas_pair <- chagas |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(subject_id), nzchar(as.character(subject_id))) |>
  dplyr::group_by(subject_id, chromatography) |>
  dplyr::summarise(m = median(log2_ratio), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = chromatography, values_from = m) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(HILIC), !is.na(RP))

OFFSET_PAIR <- median(chagas_pair$RP - chagas_pair$HILIC)
# A median of exactly zero arrives as -1e-16 and would print as "-0.00".
OFFSET_PAIR_TXT <- sprintf("%+.2f", ifelse(abs(OFFSET_PAIR) < 0.005, 0, OFFSET_PAIR))
cp <- wilcox.test(chagas_pair$RP, chagas_pair$HILIC, paired = TRUE)

knitr::kable(chagas_grp, digits = 2,
             caption = "Same subjects, same serum, two chromatographies (group level)")
knitr::kable(chagas_pair |> dplyr::mutate(difference = RP - HILIC), digits = 2,
             caption = "The same comparison, paired within subject")
```

Compared at the group level the two columns differ by
`r sprintf("%.2f", OFFSET_GRP)` log2, about
`r sprintf("%.1f", 2^OFFSET_GRP)`-fold, which looks like a reassuringly small
offset. The paired version is the design that actually holds biology fixed, and
it does not support that reading: only **`r nrow(chagas_pair)` subjects** yield
a ratio on both columns, the median difference is `r OFFSET_PAIR_TXT` log2,
reverse phase is higher in `r sum(chagas_pair$RP > chagas_pair$HILIC)` of
`r nrow(chagas_pair)`, and p = `r sprintf("%.2f", cp$p.value)`. The per-subject
differences run from
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(chagas_pair$RP - chagas_pair$HILIC))` to
`r sprintf("%+.1f", max(chagas_pair$RP - chagas_pair$HILIC))` log2.

So the honest conclusion is not "the offset is 1.5-fold". It is that the one
direct measurement available puts the **central** offset near zero while leaving
it very imprecisely determined, on six subjects. That is not a licence to pool
absolute ratios across deposits. It does mean the interesting cross-cohort ratio
work has to come from designs where the offset cannot enter at all, which is
what follows.

### The matrix contrast that carries no offset at all

The cleanest comparison in the corpus needs no correction whatsoever. Within the
probe study the **same 14 subjects** gave plasma and urine, on the same
instrument, in the same run. Any response factor is shared and cancels exactly
in a paired test.

```{r ratio-paired-matrix}
# Same canonical vocabulary as Part A, then restricted to the matrices that can
# actually carry a ratio.
ratio_pf$site <- canon_site(ratio_pf$body_site)
ratio_pf$site[!ratio_pf$site %in% c("plasma", "serum", "urine", "faeces")] <- NA

paired <- ratio_pf |>
  dplyr::filter(study == "Jarmusch probe (082493 + 084008)",
                site %in% c("plasma", "urine")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(subject_id, site) |>
  dplyr::summarise(m = median(log2_ratio), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = site, values_from = m) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(plasma), !is.na(urine))

pw   <- wilcox.test(paired$plasma, paired$urine, paired = TRUE)
gap  <- median(paired$plasma - paired$urine)
```

Across `r nrow(paired)` subjects the plasma ratio exceeds the urine ratio in
**`r sum(paired$plasma > paired$urine)` of `r nrow(paired)`**, by a median of
`r sprintf("%.2f", gap)` log2 (`r sprintf("%.0f", 2^gap)`-fold), paired Wilcoxon
p = `r sprintf("%.2g", pw$p.value)`. The parent dominates in blood and the
metabolite dominates in urine, which is the textbook disposition of an
extensively metabolised drug, recovered from public data with no targeted assay
and with the offset arithmetically removed.

### Does the ordering survive across independent studies?

Now the harder question: does the same ordering appear when the cohorts are not
the same people? Only study-by-matrix cells backed by at least five subjects are
interpretable; the rest rest on a single subject and are listed only for
completeness.

```{r ratio-by-study-matrix}
cell <- ratio_pf |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(site)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(site, study) |>
  dplyr::summarise(files = dplyr::n(), subjects = dplyr::n_distinct(subject_id),
                   median_log2 = median(log2_ratio), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(usable = subjects >= 5) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(usable), median_log2)

knitr::kable(cell, digits = 2,
             caption = "log2(parent / metabolite) per body site and independent study")

vc <- ratio_pf |> dplyr::filter(site %in% c("plasma", "serum", "urine"))
av <- anova(lm(log2_ratio ~ site + factor(study), data = vc))
ss <- av[["Sum Sq"]]
var_tbl <- data.frame(term = c("body site", "study, given body site", "residual"),
                      pct_variance = round(100 * ss / sum(ss), 1))

# An interval on the split, resampling STUDIES rather than files. The two
# components are properties of a corpus of a few studies, not of its files, and a
# file-level bootstrap would report a precision the design does not have. A study
# drawn twice enters as two studies, or the resample is a subsample.
set.seed(1)
.st <- unique(vc$study)
.vboot <- replicate(2000, {
  d <- sample(.st, replace = TRUE)
  z <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(d), function(j) {
    x <- vc[vc$study == d[j], , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(x)) x$study <- paste0(j, "|", x$study)
    x
  }))
  if (dplyr::n_distinct(z$site) < 2 || dplyr::n_distinct(z$study) < 2)
    return(rep(NA_real_, 3))
  a2 <- anova(lm(log2_ratio ~ site + factor(study), data = z))
  if (nrow(a2) < 3) return(rep(NA_real_, 3))
  s2 <- a2[["Sum Sq"]]
  100 * s2[seq_len(3)] / sum(s2)
})
var_tbl$ci_95 <- sprintf("%.1f to %.1f",
                         apply(.vboot, 1, quantile, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
                         apply(.vboot, 1, quantile, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE))
var_tbl$usable_resamples <- sum(!is.na(.vboot[1, ]))
knitr::kable(var_tbl, caption = paste(
  "Variance in the ratio attributable to matrix versus study.",
  "Intervals are a bootstrap over studies, the unit the components describe."))
```

The four usable cells order urine below plasma below serum, and the plasma cells
from two unrelated studies (the probe cohort and MTBLS1866) bracket zero while
the serum cell sits well above it. That ordering is suggestive but it is **not**
a test: each cell still carries its own offset, and the serum column is one
study. The variance decomposition is the part that does carry weight, because it
does not depend on any single cell being correctly calibrated: body site
accounts for about four times more of the ratio's variance than study identity
does. The bootstrap intervals overlap, so the honest reading is that the study
term is small rather than absent -- but whatever the per-deposit offsets are,
they are not what is organising this data. Three quarters of the variance sits
within cells, which is where a biological signal would have to live and where
this design cannot look for it.

### What this does and does not license

The one thing here that stands on its own is the **paired matrix contrast**,
because the offset is arithmetically absent rather than assumed small. The
variance decomposition supports it. The cross-study ordering is consistent with
it. Read together, the ratio gives a **disposition readout**: parent-dominant in
blood, metabolite-dominant in urine. Part B continues to use within-study
contrasts, where no offset can enter at all.

Four things this does not license, three of which looked like results until they
were checked:

- **Pooling absolute ratios across deposits, or ranking deposits by ratio.** The
  offset was not successfully measured above, only bounded loosely. The original
  constraint stands.
- **Dosed probe versus incidental exposure.** Pooled, the two differ strongly
  (medians 0.52 and 2.31, Wilcoxon p = 3e-11). But the entire "dosed" arm is
  MSV000082493 and MSV000084008, which is **one study under two accessions**.
  The comparison is one study against eight, and the apparent significance is a
  pseudo-replicated single cohort. It is not a finding.
- **Reverse phase versus HILIC.** Pooled, these also differ strongly (p =
  2e-11), but HILIC here is almost entirely serum and reverse phase almost
  entirely plasma, so that test measures matrix, not method. The controlled
  version, the same subjects on both columns above, is null and points the other
  way.
- **The metabolite channel remains isomer-exposed.** Omeprazole sulfone shares
  the metabolite's formula and precursor mass. The urine result is the ratio's
  largest effect and sits in the channel most vulnerable to it, so it is
  reported as disposition consistent with pharmacology, not as a quantified
  metabolite concentration.

# Every field, both read-outs

The scan above asks whether propagation *enables* a contrast, comparing what MS2
could test against what MS1 can. This section asks the different question the
workflow was built for: given everything the corpus records, what does it
actually show. Every deposit is crossed with every field that divides it, and
each combination is tested twice — once on presence, once on the ratio.

Two joins have to be right or the whole scan is noise. `metrics_*` carries
cache-prefixed file names, so the key needs `norm_file_key(x, bio_files)`; the
bare form leaves the accession on MetaboLights names and the join silently
returns almost nothing. And `load_metadata()` can describe more files than the
deposit contributed — MSV000091520 lists 2,732 rows against 2,144 extracted
files — so the metadata is restricted to the extraction set before anything is
counted.

```{r scan-build}
#| echo: false
BIO <- readRDS("artifacts/bio_files_per_ds.rds")
SFIELDS <- c("sex", "age", "health_status", "body_site", "country", "treatment")

scan_pf <- function(ds) {
  r <- readRDS(sprintf("artifacts/per_dataset/%s.rds", ds))
  m <- merge(as.data.frame(r$metrics_par), as.data.frame(r$metrics_met),
             by = "file", all = TRUE)
  pd <- m$par_detected %in% TRUE; md <- m$met_detected %in% TRUE
  d <- data.frame(k = norm_file_key(m$file, BIO[[ds]]), par = pd, met = md,
                  l2 = ifelse(pd & md, log2(m$par_auc / m$met_auc), NA_real_))
  meta <- tryCatch(load_metadata(ds), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(meta) || !nrow(meta)) meta <- as.data.frame(r$sample_tbl)
  meta$k <- norm_file_key(meta$file, BIO[[ds]])
  meta <- meta[meta$k %in% norm_file_key(BIO[[ds]], BIO[[ds]]), ]
  meta <- meta[!duplicated(meta$k), ]
  i <- match(meta$k, d$k)
  meta$par <- d$par[i] %in% TRUE; meta$met <- d$met[i] %in% TRUE
  meta$l2 <- d$l2[i]; meta$ds <- ds
  meta
}
scan_all <- bind_rows(lapply(names(BIO), function(x)
  tryCatch(scan_pf(x), error = function(e) {
    message("scan_pf failed for ", x, ": ", conditionMessage(e)); NULL })))
stopifnot(nrow(scan_all) > 0)
scan_all <- scan_all[!(scan_all$ds == "MSV000082493" &
                       grepl("plasma|blood", tolower(scan_all$body_site))), ]
cat(nrow(scan_all), "files |", n_distinct(scan_all$ds), "deposits | detected: parent",
    sum(scan_all$par), "metabolite", sum(scan_all$met), "both",
    sum(scan_all$par & scan_all$met), "\n")
```

## What unit each deposit supports

A contrast needs independent observations, so files have to be collapsed to
people wherever the deposit records who they came from. Nine of the twelve do.
What varies is how the identifier behaves, and the differences are not cosmetic:
it may repeat, because the person was sampled more than once; it may appear
exactly once, because the study drew one sample per participant; or it may cover
only part of the deposit. Only the last of those is a real obstacle. A test that
asked merely whether the identifier repeats would reject six of the nine.

```{r scan-units}
#| echo: false
unit_of <- function(x) {
  sid <- if ("subject_id" %in% names(x)) x$subject_id else rep(NA, nrow(x))
  sib <- unlist(sibling_id_map[unique(x$ds)], use.names = FALSE)
  ok <- !is.na(sid) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(sid)))
  lab <- sum(ok); nsub <- n_distinct(sid[ok]); reps <- if (nsub) lab / nsub else NA
  if (!lab) list("file", "no subject id recorded")
  else if (lab < nrow(x))
    list(if (subject_resolved(sid, sibling_ids = sib)) "subject (partial)" else "file",
         sprintf("id on %d of %d files, %d subjects", lab, nrow(x), nsub))
  else if (nsub == nrow(x)) list("subject", sprintf("%d subjects, one sample each", nsub))
  else list("subject", {
    # Median and range, not the mean: a mean of "5.1 files each" describes no
    # subject, and it hid that MSV000084008 runs 9 to 36 files per person.
    .k <- as.integer(table(sid[ok]))
    sprintf("%d subjects, %d files each (%d-%d)", nsub,
            as.integer(stats::median(.k)), min(.k), max(.k))
  })
}
units <- bind_rows(lapply(split(scan_all, scan_all$ds), function(x) {
  u <- unit_of(x)
  data.frame(deposit = short_ds(x$ds[1]), files = nrow(x),
             unit = u[[1]], reason = u[[2]])
}))
knitr::kable(units, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "The analysis unit each deposit can support, and why")
```

Three deposits support repeated measures on the same people; four are
cross-sectional, one sample per participant; two label part of the deposit and
are corroborated by their sibling; three record nobody. Only that last group is
analysed at file level, and those results are exploratory in the strict sense —
the files are not independent observations and a p-value on them overstates the
evidence. They are still worth computing, because a contrast that fails even at
file level cannot be rescued by a stricter unit.

## The scan

Presence is tested with Fisher's exact test on categorical fields and logistic
regression on continuous ones; the ratio with a linear model on the files
carrying both compounds. Benjamini-Hochberg control is applied within each
read-out.

```{r scan-run}
#| echo: false
set.seed(1)
scan_rows <- list()
for (ds in unique(scan_all$ds)) {
  x0 <- scan_all[scan_all$ds == ds, ]
  u <- unit_of(x0)
  x <- if (u[[1]] == "subject")
    x0 |> group_by(subject_id) |>
      summarise(par = any(par), met = any(met), l2 = median(l2[is.finite(l2)]),
                across(any_of(SFIELDS), ~ .x[1]), .groups = "drop") |> as.data.frame()
    else x0
  for (f in intersect(SFIELDS, names(x))) {
    v <- x[[f]]; keep <- !is.na(v) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(v)))
    if (sum(keep) < 8) next
    xf <- x[keep, ]; vv <- v[keep]
    num <- !any(is.na(as_num(vv)))
    cont <- num && n_distinct(vv) > 12
    if (!cont) {
      tb <- table(vv); if (length(tb) < 2 || sum(tb >= 3) < 2) next
      vv <- factor(vv)
    } else vv <- as_num(vv)
    for (rl in c("par", "met", "either")) {
      y <- if (rl == "either") (xf$par | xf$met) else xf[[rl]]
      if (n_distinct(y) < 2) next
      pv <- tryCatch(if (cont)
          summary(glm(y ~ vv, family = binomial))$coefficients[2, 4]
        else fisher.test(table(vv, y), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)$p.value,
        error = function(e) NA_real_)
      scan_rows[[length(scan_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        deposit = short_ds(ds), unit = u[[1]], field = f, readout = "presence",
        role = rl, n = nrow(xf), det = sum(y), est = NA_real_, p = pv)
    }
    r2 <- xf[is.finite(xf$l2), ]
    if (nrow(r2) >= 6) {
      v2 <- if (cont) as_num(r2[[f]]) else factor(r2[[f]])
      if (cont || n_distinct(v2) >= 2) {
        co <- tryCatch(summary(lm(r2$l2 ~ v2))$coefficients, error = function(e) NULL)
        if (!is.null(co) && nrow(co) >= 2)
          scan_rows[[length(scan_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
            deposit = short_ds(ds), unit = u[[1]], field = f, readout = "ratio",
            role = "both", n = nrow(r2), det = nrow(r2), est = co[2, 1], p = co[2, 4])
      }
    }
  }
}
SC <- bind_rows(scan_rows)
SC$q <- NA_real_
for (rd in unique(SC$readout)) {
  i <- SC$readout == rd & !is.na(SC$p)
  SC$q[i] <- p.adjust(SC$p[i], "BH")
}
knitr::kable(SC |> group_by(field, readout) |>
               summarise(tests = n(), significant = sum(q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                         .groups = "drop"),
             caption = "Tests run and how many survive FDR, by field and read-out")
```

```{r scan-significant}
#| echo: false
sig <- SC[!is.na(SC$q) & SC$q < 0.05, ]
knitr::kable(sig[order(sig$q), c("deposit","unit","field","readout","role","n","det","q")],
             row.names = FALSE, digits = 4,
             caption = "Every contrast surviving FDR 0.05")
```

Two things stand out, and both are replications rather than single findings.
Clinical group separates detection in two unrelated COVID cohorts, MTBLS1866 in
Italy and MTBLS11656 in China, neither of which knows about the other. Age does
the same in two unrelated serum cohorts, the Chagas study and ST002044 in India.
A single deposit showing an effect is a hypothesis; the same effect in a second
cohort collected by different people for a different reason is the argument this
workflow exists to make.

The negative is as informative. **No ratio contrast survives FDR anywhere in the
corpus**, against presence contrasts that do — the quantitative read-out
validated in `04` does not travel, exactly as the body-site and cross-study
analyses predict. And sex is null in every deposit that records it.


# Part B: The quantitative strand, and its limits

Part A is the field's prevalence analysis, made more sensitive. Part B is the
piece the field does not have: turning the propagated detections into a
quantitative, error-controlled cross-cohort analysis, borrowing directly from
how proteomics handles the identical problem.

## The within-study contrast (the quantitative strand)

Where a cohort supports it, the within-study contrast (defined above: the offset
cancels in a within-cohort difference) is the quantitative unit that *could* be
pooled. We compute it per cohort here; the pooling itself is deferred for the
reasons in the final section.

## Defining the contrast

For each dataset we restrict to samples where both compounds were detected, pick
the grouping variable the dataset can actually support, collapse it to two
levels ("case" vs "reference"), and fit a linear model of `log2_ratio` on that
grouping. The coefficient is the contrast.

```{r within-study-fn}
fit_within_study <- function(df) {

  df_both <- df %>% filter(detection_tier == "both", is.finite(log2_ratio))
  if (nrow(df_both) < 6) {
    return(tibble(contrast = NA_character_, estimate = NA_real_,
                  se = NA_real_, n = nrow(df_both), note = "n<6"))
  }

  # Try stratifiers in priority order; first usable one wins. This ordering is
  # the weak point of the whole section: see the final discussion.
  candidates <- c("health_status", "group", "sex", "country", "body_site")
  picked <- NULL
  for (v in candidates) {
    if (!v %in% names(df_both)) next
    counts <- df_both %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[v]])) %>% count(.data[[v]])
    if (nrow(counts) >= 2 && all(counts$n >= 3)) { picked <- v; break }
  }
  if (is.null(picked)) {
    return(tibble(contrast = NA_character_, estimate = NA_real_,
                  se = NA_real_, n = nrow(df_both), note = "no_stratifier"))
  }

  # Collapse to two levels: the smallest group becomes "case", so the estimate
  # reads as "case minus reference".
  df_both <- df_both %>%
    mutate(
      .v    = .data[[picked]],
      .case = .v == names(sort(table(.v)))[1],
      .grp  = factor(ifelse(.case, "case", "ref"), levels = c("ref", "case"))
    )

  m <- lm(log2_ratio ~ .grp, data = df_both)
  coefs <- summary(m)$coefficients
  tibble(
    contrast = paste0(picked, ": ", names(sort(table(df_both$.v)))[1], " vs rest"),
    estimate = coefs[".grpcase", "Estimate"],
    se       = coefs[".grpcase", "Std. Error"],
    n        = nrow(df_both),
    note     = NA_character_
  )
}
```

## The effect-size table

```{r per-study-effects}
effects <- samples %>%
  group_by(dataset_id) %>%
  group_modify(~ fit_within_study(.x)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(datasets %>% select(dataset_id, repository, chromatography,
                                const_country, const_body_site),
            by = "dataset_id") %>%
  arrange(dataset_id)

effects
write_csv(effects, "artifacts/meta_effects.csv")
```

### What each column means

An **effect size** is just a number that says how big a difference is, expressed
so that it can be compared with the same number from another study. Many fields
use a standardised effect size (Cohen's d, Hedges' g), which divides the
difference by its spread so that studies measuring different things on different
scales can be put side by side. **We deliberately do not standardise here.** Our
readout is already on a common and directly interpretable scale: `log2_ratio` is
in doublings, and the response-factor offset cancels in the subtraction. So the
raw difference in log2 units *is* the effect size, and it means the same thing
in every dataset. Standardising would divide by a within-dataset spread that
varies for reasons (cohort heterogeneity, sample size) that have nothing to do
with the biology, and would make the studies less comparable rather than more.

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `dataset_id` | the (deposit, assay) entity |
| `contrast` | which grouping variable was used, and which level was treated as "case". `sex: female vs rest` and `health_status: severe vs rest` are **not the same question**, which matters a great deal below |
| `estimate` | the contrast itself: mean `log2(par/met)` in the case group minus the reference group. Units are log2, so `+1` means the parent-to-metabolite ratio is twice as high in the case group; `0` means no difference; negative means the case group has relatively more metabolite (faster apparent metabolism) |
| `se` | standard error of that estimate: how precisely we know it. Small `se` means a tight estimate. A rough 95% interval is `estimate ± 1.96 × se`. Any pooling would weight studies by this |
| `n` | number of both-tier samples the fit used. With `n` in single digits, `se` is large and the estimate is weak |
| `note` | why a dataset has no estimate: `n<6` (too few usable samples) or `no_stratifier` (no grouping variable with two levels of at least three samples) |
| `repository`, `chromatography`, `const_country`, `const_body_site` | dataset-level attributes, available as moderators for a future pooled model |

## Per-study contrast, ordered

```{r exp-effect-bars, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5}
fit_eff <- effects |> filter(!is.na(estimate), !is.na(se))

eff_plot <- fit_eff |>
  mutate(ci_lo = estimate - 1.96 * se,
         ci_hi = estimate + 1.96 * se,
         ds    = fct_reorder(short_ds(dataset_id), estimate))

ggplot(eff_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = ds)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi), orientation = "y",
                width = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = chromatography), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), hjust = -0.25, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "contrast: case minus reference, log2(parent / metabolite)",
       y = NULL, colour = "chrom.",
       title = "Per-study contrast with 95% confidence interval") +
  theme_bw()
```

Here the intervals are wide, most of them cross zero, and, critically, the
contrasts on the y-axis are **not all asking the same question**. Read this as a
description of what each dataset happens to offer, not as a set of comparable
results.

## Does the ratio itself track sex, health or age across the corpus?

Part A pooled *presence*, which is a rate and needs no common scale. The obvious
next question is whether the *ratio* moves with the covariates the corpus
records most often, pooled across all cohorts rather than one cohort at a time.
This is the analysis the offset argument above predicts will fail, so it is
worth running rather than asserting.

Two models are fitted for each covariate. The first pools every subject and
ignores which study they came from, which is what a naive corpus analysis would
do. The second adds a study term, which absorbs the per-cohort offset and leaves
only the within-cohort information — the same logic as the within-study
contrast, but pooled. If a covariate effect is real it should survive the study
term; if it is the offset in disguise, it will not.

```{r ratio-covariate-recover}
# Chagas records subject, sex, age and infection status in its file names and
# only partly in the catalogue. The recovery is validated rather than assumed:
# where the catalogue does carry a subject id the parsed one agrees 158/158, sex
# differs only in encoding and age by at most a year. It is local to this
# section, so Chagas unit counts differ from Part A.
rq <- pm[pm$detection_tier %in% "both" & is.finite(pm$log2_ratio), ]
ch_pat <- "^(pos|neg)_(inf|uninf|non)[_a-z]*_([0-9]+)(_[0-9]+)?_(female|male)_([0-9]+)_.*$"
ch <- rq$study == "Chagas serum" & grepl(ch_pat, rq$fk)
rq$subj[ch] <- sub(ch_pat, "\\3", rq$fk[ch])
rq$sex2[ch] <- sub(ch_pat, "\\5", rq$fk[ch])
rq$agen[ch] <- as_num(sub(ch_pat, "\\6", rq$fk[ch]))
rq$clin[ch] <- ifelse(sub(ch_pat, "\\2", rq$fk[ch]) == "uninf",
                      "uninfected", "T. cruzi infected")
rq <- rq[!(rq$study == "Chagas serum" & grepl("_qc_", rq$fk)), ]

rq$health <- harmonise_health(rq$clin)

# The unit rule again: one ratio per subject per matrix, median over that
# subject's files. A cohort sampling 16 files per person must not outvote a
# cohort sampling one.
ru <- rq |>
  dplyr::mutate(unit = ifelse(is.na(subj), paste0("file:", fk),
                              paste(study, subj, site))) |>
  dplyr::group_by(unit) |>
  dplyr::summarise(study = dplyr::first(study), site = dplyr::first(site),
                   l2 = median(log2_ratio), sex2 = dplyr::first(sex2),
                   health = dplyr::first(health), agen = dplyr::first(agen),
                   .groups = "drop")
```

```{r ratio-covariate-audit}
# The health mapping is printed rather than trusted: every clinical label in the
# corpus, and which side of the binary it was put on.
rq |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(clin)) |>
  dplyr::count(study, clin, health, name = "files") |>
  dplyr::arrange(study)
```

```{r ratio-covariate-scan}
# Restricted to blood, because matrix moves the ratio by more than any covariate
# tested here (plasma vs urine is about -2.6 log2) and would otherwise dominate.
blood <- ru[ru$site %in% c("plasma", "serum"), ]

scan_cov <- function(dat, v, label) {
  z <- dat[!is.na(dat[[v]]), ]
  if (nrow(z) < 8) return(NULL)
  naive <- summary(lm(as.formula(paste("l2 ~", v)), data = z))$coefficients
  adj   <- summary(lm(as.formula(paste("l2 ~ study +", v)), data = z))$coefficients
  ra <- grep(paste0("^", v), rownames(adj))[1]
  tibble(covariate = label, units = nrow(z), studies = dplyr::n_distinct(z$study),
         est_naive = round(naive[2, 1], 2), p_naive = signif(naive[2, 4], 2),
         est_adj   = round(adj[ra, 1], 2),  p_adj   = signif(adj[ra, 4], 2),
         p_study   = signif(anova(lm(as.formula(paste("l2 ~ study +", v)),
                                     data = z))["study", "Pr(>F)"], 2))
}

ratio_cov <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  scan_cov(blood, "sex2",   "sex (male vs female)"),
  scan_cov(blood, "health", "not healthy vs healthy"),
  scan_cov(blood, "agen",   "age (per year)"))
ratio_cov
write_csv(ratio_cov, "artifacts/ratio_covariates.csv")
```

```{r ratio-covariate-confound}
# How much of "healthy vs not" is really "one deposit vs another"? If each
# health arm sits almost entirely in its own study, the contrast and the offset
# are the same number. The within-cohort version is the check: only a study
# containing BOTH arms can separate them.
hb <- blood[!is.na(blood$health), ]
health_by_study <- hb |> dplyr::count(study, health) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = health, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
health_by_study

both_arms <- health_by_study$study[
  health_by_study$healthy >= 3 & health_by_study$`not healthy` >= 3]
within_health <- lapply(both_arms, function(s) {
  z <- hb[hb$study == s, ]
  # same direction as the model coefficient: not healthy minus healthy
  tibble(study = s, units = nrow(z),
         est = round(unname(diff(tapply(z$l2, z$health, median))), 2),
         p   = signif(wilcox.test(l2 ~ health, data = z)$p.value, 2))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
within_health
```

Nothing survives the study term. Sex moves the ratio by
`r sprintf("%+.2f", ratio_cov$est_naive[1])` log2 pooled ($p =
`r ratio_cov$p_naive[1]`$) and by `r sprintf("%+.2f", ratio_cov$est_adj[1])`
once study is accounted for ($p = `r ratio_cov$p_adj[1]`$). Age is flat either
way ($p = `r ratio_cov$p_naive[3]`$ and $p = `r ratio_cov$p_adj[3]`$).

Health status is the one covariate that looks significant, and it is the most
instructive result in this section. Pooled across the corpus and ignoring which
deposit each subject came from, unhealthy subjects sit
`r sprintf("%+.2f", ratio_cov$est_naive[2])` log2 below the healthy ones at $p =
`r ratio_cov$p_naive[2]`$ — a result that, reported on its own, would read as a
real corpus-level finding. Adding the study term leaves the estimate essentially
unchanged at `r sprintf("%+.2f", ratio_cov$est_adj[2])` but takes the $p$ value
to `r ratio_cov$p_adj[2]`, while the study term itself is significant at $p =
`r ratio_cov$p_study[2]`$.

An estimate that survives adjustment while its $p$ value does not is the
signature of confounding rather than of a real effect losing power. Health status
in this corpus is almost entirely a between-study variable, as the table above
shows: each arm sits largely in its own deposit, so comparing healthy against
unhealthy mostly compares one deposit against another, and the offset is exactly
what that comparison picks up. Only a cohort holding both arms can separate the
two, and
`r if (!nrow(within_health)) "no cohort in the corpus holds both" else paste0(if (nrow(within_health) == 1) "the single cohort that does gives " else paste0("the ", nrow(within_health), " that do give "), sprintf("%+.2f", within_health$est[1]), " log2 at $p = ", within_health$p[1], "$ on ", within_health$units[1], " subjects")`.
The direction agrees with the pooled estimate but the significance does not
survive, which is the whole point: the corpus-wide result is not evidence that
illness changes the
hydroxylation ratio; it is evidence that the deposits differ from each other,
which is what the offset argument said all along.

The result is negative but not final. It rests on `r nrow(blood)` blood subjects
across `r dplyr::n_distinct(blood$study)` studies, because a ratio needs both
compounds in the same file. Two things would enlarge it: deeper metadata, since
the Chagas recovery above shows deposits were set aside on what the catalogues
indexed rather than on what the submitters actually recorded; and deposits that
contain both arms of a contrast, since a clinical stratum that is also a deposit
cannot be separated from that deposit's offset by any amount of pooling.

# Chagas HILIC vs RP: one direct check

MSV000092754 (HILIC) and MSV000092757 (reverse phase) are paired deposits from
the same Chagas serum study: the same subjects and blood draws, run on two
chromatographies, matched by `codigo_num`. It is the only place in the corpus
where we can watch the same biology measured two ways, which makes it the one
direct check on the offset argument above.

```{r chagas-pair}
#| echo: false
HILIC_DS <- "MSV000092754"
RP_DS    <- "MSV000092757"

per_subject_ratio <- function(ds) {
  samples %>%
    filter(dataset_id == ds, detection_tier == "both",
           !par_fwhm_outlier %in% TRUE, !met_fwhm_outlier %in% TRUE,
           is.finite(log2_ratio)) %>%
    group_by(subject_id) %>%
    summarise(log2_ratio    = median(log2_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
              health_status = dplyr::first(health_status),
              .groups       = "drop")
}

chagas <- dplyr::inner_join(
  per_subject_ratio(HILIC_DS) %>% dplyr::rename(log2_ratio_HILIC = log2_ratio),
  per_subject_ratio(RP_DS)    %>% dplyr::select(subject_id, log2_ratio_RP = log2_ratio),
  by = "subject_id")

cat("Subjects matched across both chromatographies:", nrow(chagas), "\n")
```

```{r chagas-paired, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5}
if (nrow(chagas) >= 3) {
  chagas |>
    pivot_longer(c(log2_ratio_HILIC, log2_ratio_RP),
                 names_to = "chromatography", values_to = "log2_ratio") |>
    mutate(chromatography = sub("log2_ratio_", "", chromatography)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = chromatography, y = log2_ratio,
               group = subject_id, colour = health_status)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "log2(parent / metabolite)", colour = "health status",
         title = "Per-subject log2 ratio on HILIC and reverse phase, MSV000092754 / MSV000092757") +
    theme_bw()
}
```

**What this can and cannot tell us.** Only a handful of subjects survive the
requirement of a usable ratio in *both* chromatographies, so this is a look, not
a test. Correlation coefficients, Bland-Altman limits of agreement and
heteroscedasticity slopes on this many points would report precision we do not
have, so we do not compute them.

What the picture is good for is direction. If the lines were roughly parallel,
each subject shifting by a similar amount between the two methods, that is the
constant-additive-offset behaviour the previous section assumes, and it would
support the claim that the offset cancels in a within-study contrast. If instead
the lines cross each other freely, the readout depends on the chromatography in
a way a single constant cannot absorb, and every cross-method claim in the
project needs a louder caveat. Judge it by eye, and treat it as one encouraging
or discouraging data point rather than as a validation.

# What a meta-analysis could add, and what it needs first

The obvious next step is to pool the per-study contrasts into a single
cross-cohort estimate: a random-effects meta-analysis, weighting each dataset by
its precision, reporting a pooled contrast with a confidence interval plus τ²
and I² to quantify how much the cohorts genuinely disagree. That is the standard
tool and it is the right shape for this data. **We are not running it yet, on
purpose.**

**Why not.** A meta-analysis pools estimates that answer the same question. Look
again at the `contrast` column: because `fit_within_study()` walks a priority
list and takes the first usable grouping, most datasets end up contributing a
**sex** contrast, simply because sex is the one variable that is populated
nearly everywhere. Pooling "severe versus healthy" from one study together with
"male versus female" from another does not estimate anything. Run anyway it
returns a tidy-looking pooled value with a narrow interval and I² near zero,
which is worse than no answer because it looks like a result. The blocker is not
the statistics; it is that the corpus does not supply a shared, biologically
meaningful contrast across enough datasets.

**What would make it work**, roughly in order of value:

- **Pick one question and only include datasets that can answer it.** For
  example health status or disease severity, dropping every dataset without it.
  Fewer studies, but a pooled number that means something.
- **Handle the censored samples.** `parent_only` and `metab_only` are ratio
  observations with one bound known. An interval-censored (Tobit-style) model
  uses them as bounds instead of discarding them, which matters because they are
  exactly the most extreme ratios, and dropping them shrinks any effect toward
  zero.
- **Decide how to treat the method.** Chromatography, instrument and biofluid
  all reset the offset. With a real pooled model these become moderators or
  subgroups. Note the corpus currently has at least two deposits whose recorded
  chromatography is doubtful given their retention times, so this needs the
  metadata fixed before it can be trusted.
- **Consider the one-stage alternative.** Rather than fitting each study then
  pooling, a hierarchical (mixed-effects) model on the sample-level data with a
  random effect per dataset uses the individual samples directly, which is
  generally better behaved when per-study `n` is small, as it is here.
- **Pool a robust quantity, never raw abundance.** This is settled practice, and
  it converges across fields. Cross-repository proteomics meta-analyses of
  independent public deposits (e.g. the 12-dataset colorectal-cancer study,
  PMC10833860) uniformly re-process the raw files and then pool a
  distribution-free quantity: rank-binned abundances there, Stouffer/Fisher
  p-value combination in MetaMSD, within-study log fold-changes in the
  metabolomics tool MetaHD. If we ever pool a ratio across cohorts, it must be
  rank-transformed or reduced to a per-cohort statistic first, for the same
  response-factor reason that forbids pooling the raw ratio. That these
  cross-repository quantitative meta-analyses exist and work is also the point:
  our contribution is not the pooling, which is standard, but using MS1
  propagation to *produce* the per-cohort quantity that the reverse-metabolomics
  / MASST world does not generate.
- **Do not treat every accession as an independent cohort.** `01` records the
  known exceptions in `artifacts/related_deposits.csv`. Today it contains one:
  **MSV000084008 is a re-deposit of MSV000082493's blood arm**, and both come
  from the same 14 subjects (PMC7485946). They contribute different biofluids
  here, so both are kept, but pooling them as two studies would count those
  subjects twice and hand the pair a double vote in any precision-weighted
  estimate. A deposit accession is not a study, and any pooling has to be keyed
  on the study.
- **Be honest about country.** Each country is represented by a single dataset,
  so country and dataset are perfectly confounded. Any "country effect" is that
  one deposit's method. At best this is a calibration check against published
  CYP2C19 frequencies, never an estimate.

The prerequisite for all of it is a decision about which question the pool is
supposed to answer. That is a discussion to have as a group, not something to
settle by picking whichever variable happens to be populated.

# Appendix: one study, two accessions (MSV000082493 and MSV000084008)

```{r appendix-overlap}
#| echo: false
N_SHARED_APPX <- length(intersect(
  norm_file_key(samples_perfile$file[samples_perfile$dataset_id == "MSV000082493"]),
  norm_file_key(samples_perfile$file[samples_perfile$dataset_id == "MSV000084008"])))
```

These two deposits are **not independent cohorts**. They are the same study,
submitted twice:

- The same **14 subjects**, and on every file present in both, `subject_id`
  agrees: `r N_SHARED_APPX` of `r N_SHARED_APPX`.
- **`r N_SHARED_APPX` files are shared between them** - all `blood_plasma`.
  Where both yield a parent detection, the AUC correlation is **1.000** and the
  median relative difference is **0**; the largest single difference is 11%, so
  most are the same raw file and a few differ slightly (most likely
  re-conversion, not different samples). Both deposits are RP.
- 082493 additionally holds the multi-matrix collection (390 skin, 148 fecal,
  139 urine, 8 plasma); 084008 holds 106 plasma files 082493 does not. Neither
  is a subset of the other, so distinct plasma across both is 447.

Nothing in the repository metadata signals this. Different accessions, separate
submissions, no cross-reference. It surfaced only from a duplicate-file audit.

**This inflates any public-data meta-analysis, and it hits an MS2-only analysis
harder than ours**, because the duplicated files are exactly the plasma where
MASST found the parent:

| counted over | summed | distinct | inflation |
|---|---|---|---|
| parent MS2 hit files | 389 | 233 | **+67%** |
| 5-OH MS2 hit files | 494 | 342 | **+44%** |
| all MS2 hit files, corpus | 668 | 472 | **+42%** |

So a classic reverse-metabolomics presence analysis reporting "N public files
contain the drug" would over-report by roughly half on this pair alone. That is
a property of the data ecosystem, not of any particular method, and it is not
routinely checked.

## A shared file name does not always mean a duplicate

The opposite case exists in this same corpus and is just as dangerous.
**MSV000092754 and MSV000092757 share all 164 file names** (`pos_QC_1.mzXML` and
so on) and the same 79 subjects, but 092754 is HILIC and 092757 is RP: the same
samples on two columns, submitted as separate accessions. Their extracted values
differ by up to **117x**. De-duplicating those by file name would merge a HILIC
run into an RP run and delete 164 real files.

So file name identity means two opposite things here, and only the analytical
context distinguishes them:

| pair | file names | chromatography | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 082493 / 084008 | 333 shared | RP / RP | same files - **collapse** |
| 092754 / 092757 | 164 shared | HILIC / RP | different runs - **keep apart** |

**What we therefore do**, and it must be stated wherever these numbers appear:

1. **Identify the duplicate pair from subject identity**, not file names: the
   same 14 subjects, with subject, timepoint, study day and body site agreeing
   on 461 of 461 shared files. File names cannot make this call - here they
   indicate a duplicate, in 092754/092757 they indicate a collision.
2. **Collapse that pair, and only that pair, on file name** (`DUP_STUDY` below).
   Every other dataset stays namespaced by its own accession.
3. **Treat 082493 + 084008 as one study.** Per-cohort tables keep both
   accessions for provenance, but they must never be read as two independent
   replications - and a result "confirmed" in both is confirmed once.
4. **Re-run the collision audit when datasets are added.** Compare extracted
   AUCs for every shared key across every dataset pair: agreement means one
   file deposited twice, disagreement means two files that happen to share a
   name. Nothing else separates the two cases reliably.

One thing this does **not** address, and which is worth stating rather than
hiding: each deposit also contains **technical replicates** - 237 rows in each
of 082493 and 084008 repeat a `(subject, timepoint, day, body_site)`
combination. Those are multiple injections of one specimen, and they are counted
individually in every file-level number here, including the gain. A
specimen-level count would be more defensible, but it needs an identifier for
the specimen rather than for the person, and no deposit records one: the three
that repeat a subject do not distinguish a re-injection from a second draw, and
the rest have one file per person, so it cannot be done corpus-wide.

Subject-level analyses were never affected: the project already takes one
measure per subject, and the subject IDs agree across the two accessions.

```{r dedup-corpus}
#| echo: false
fk_all <- fkey(samples_perfile$file)
dk_all <- paste0(samples_perfile$dataset_id, "|", fk_all)
cat("files summed across datasets :", length(dk_all), "\n")
cat("distinct physical files      :", length(unique(fk_all)), "\n")
cat("counted more than once       :", length(dk_all) - length(unique(fk_all)), "\n")
```
